MR. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Now, I request Shri Yerrannaidu to speak. You have only five minutes’ time. 

SHRI KINJARAPU YERRANNAIDU Thank you Mr. Deputy-Speaker, Sir, for giving me this opportunity to speak on this Bill. 

Mr. Deputy-Speaker, Sir, this is a very important Bill. We are discussing the National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, 2004 on the floor of the House. From the Government side and from the Opposition side many speakers have spoken on this Bill. This is the UPA Government’s promise. ‘It will immediately enact a National Employment Guarantee Act. This will provide legal guarantee for at least 100 days of employment, to begin with, on asset creating public work programmes every year at minimum wages for at least one able-bodied person in rural areas, urban poor and lower middle-class households.’ This is the commitment they have given to this nation under the National Common Minimum Programme. The National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, 2004 says that in the aforesaid background, this Bill has been introduced in this Parliament. As stated in the Objects and Reasons of the Bill, the proposed legislation seeks to enhance the livelihood security of the poor households in rural areas of the country by providing at least 100 days of guaranteed wage employment to every poor household whose adult members volunteered to do unskilled manual work. They have given the promise. They have not implemented as it is. This is the failure of the UPA Government to implement the National Common Minimum Programme.

This is not a full comprehensive Bill. This is a part of the Bill. It has not mentioned about the urban poor. Members from the Congress Party, the UPA Chairperson and other senior parliamentarians have said on the floor of the House that this is a historical Bill. I will support this Bill. But how can you say that this is a historical Bill? This is an incomplete Bill which you have introduced on the floor of the House. This Bill will not be applicable to the whole country. This is not a universal Bill. 

16.02 hrs (Shri Ajay Maken in the Chair) 

According to the Objects and Reasons of this Bill, it will be implemented only in 200 districts, including in the 150 districts where the Food-for-Work programme is already implemented. After the implementation of this National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, the existing SGRY and the Food-for-Work programme, which is being implemented in 150 districts, will merge. Additionally, they are providing for only 50 districts. So, this is not a universal programme. 

For example, I am hailing from Srikakulam district. In Andhra Pradesh, we have 23 districts. According to the National Common Minimum Programme of the UPA Government, this Bill will have universal implication. But in one district, there are thousands of people who are below the poverty line having no work. They are migrating from village to urban areas. This Bill will not provide employment in those districts. This Bill will provide employment in only 200 districts. What about the other 400 districts? The Minister has to answer this. 

All right, if you say that it will be applicable to the whole country after five years means the spirit of the Bill is deviated. There are already so many wage employment programmes. There is the National Rural Employment Programme. There is RLEGP. There is Jawahar Rozgar Yojana Programme. There is Employment Assurance Programme. The Employment Assurance Programme is also a demand-driven programme but there is no legal guarantee for the poor people. Even the SGRY is also a wage employment programme to provide employment to the rural poor but there is no legal guarantee. By this Act we are giving legal guarantee for 100 days to a particular person in a poor household. But it should be applicable to the whole country. Otherwise there is no meaning in it. This is not a historical Bill. So, my Party is demanding this UPA Government that instead of waiting for five years, you have to implement this Bill in the whole country. Then only the poor people who are living below the poverty line in the rural areas will get benefit out of this Bill[m41] . 

According [e42] to this Bill, we have given power to the gram panchayat, intermediate panchayat and district panchayat. We have to strengthen these organisations. Without strengthening all these organisations, this programme would not percolate to the ground level and ultimately the poor people would not get the benefit.

For example, it has been stated that ‘a shelf of projects would be prepared by the gram sabha’. It has to be approved by the gram panchayat; then, it would be sent to the intermediate panchayat; and ultimately it reaches the district panchayat. The district panchayat would approve all these projects. To whoever applies for employment, the shelf of projects is available in the gram panchayat. For all these things, where is the infrastructure in the gram panchayat?

Throughout the country the size of the gram panchayat is not the same. In Kerala, the population of a gram panchayat is 25,000 to 30,000; in Andhra Pradesh, it is only 2,000 or 3,000. With a population of 3,000, where is the infrastructure for the gram panchayat? There is no gram panchayat which has the infrastructure. There is no village secretary. There is no infrastructure. How can they prepare a shelf of projects? The hon. Minister has to answer this because in different States, different panchayat organisations are of different sizes. If you adopt an Employment Guarantee Bill, it has to be implemented properly, with commitment, with honesty, with integrity, and without any corruption. So, the hon. Minister has to answer all these questions.

According to the UPA Manifesto, they have to include the urban poor also. If it is not possible in this Bill, the Government of India should bring in another legislation for the urban poor. It is only then that they can fulfil their promises according to the Common Minimum Programme and claim that this is a historic Bill. So, I do not agree with this claim.

In Maharashtra, they are implementing Employment Guarantee Act since 30 years. Even after 30 years, there is no shortage of migration from rural areas to urban areas. Still people are migrating to urban areas. In this situation, with these experiences, the hon. Minister should have thought in detail, in practical terms considering the way the Maharashtra Employment Guarantee Act has been implemented.

According to my party, they have to implement this measure throughout India. I told my people in my constituency: “The National Employment Guarantee Bill is coming up. You would get mandatory wage employment for 100 days in a year.” But this Bill would be applicable only in 200 districts. What can I say tomorrow to the people of my Parliamentary constituency, when those poor people approach me and ask me why they have not got employment? Where is the work to provide for them? These are some lacunae in this Bill. That is why, I humbly request that instead of implementing it in 200 districts, the Government has to implement it in all the 600 districts at a time. The hon. Minister of Panchayati Raj is also here and I hope he would agree with me.

The Government claims that this is a historic Bill. I would like to say that I support this Bill fully but it is only partly implementing the Scheme in 200 districts, which makes it old wine in a new bottle. That is why I am giving all these suggestions. The Government of India should incorporate all these suggestions. It is only then that this Bill would benefit the poor people in the rural areas and they would get 100 days’ employment legally.

SHRI A.K.S. VIJAYAN Hon. Deputy Speaker Sir, after 58 years of independence, after completing the golden jubilee celebrations and recently the freedom anniversary celebrations, we have evolved and introduced a Bill in this august House with a viable scheme that would touch the needy poor directly. I welcome the National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill. Let me express my views on behalf our party Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam while extending our support to this historic Bill.

Our leader Dr Kalaignar used to say, “We assure what we could do and we do what we assure”. Within this one and a half years of coming to power our UPA Government has ventured to implement several social welfare schemes to ameliorate poverty. The significant one among such measures is the legislation of this National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill. At the moment, when we seek to pass it in this House I would like to thank the Chairperson of our UPA Annai Sonia Gandhi and our Prime Minister Dr Manmohan Singh and the prime mover behind this governance our leader Dr Kalaignar Karunanidhi.

Our UPA Chairperson Smt. Sonia Gandhi pointed out that women would get priority while identifying the beneficiaries for this scheme and 33% of jobs guaranteed to them. I appreciate and welcome this right move. I am duty bound to bring to the notice of this august House a valid information related to this move. When Dr Kalaignar Karunanidhi was the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu, he appointed in all the 12000 panchayats 2 social welfare volunteers – a lady volunteer and also a male volunteer in each panchayat. But the Government led by Jayalalitha that came to power in 2001 retrenched all those village welfare volunteers about 25000 of them that had equal number of men and women among them. They were removed from employment so suddenly that some of them were shell-shocked and driven to suicide attempts. They were deprived of their __________________________________________________________________*Translation of the speech originally delivered in Tamil.

livelihood in a heartless fashion. I just think of UPA’s Chairperson Annai Sonia Gandhi who always thinks about the poverty stricken people of this country. I also see in her a compassionate leader championing the cause of women at the national capital. But I find another lady leader in Tamil Nadu who takes away even hard won jobs of women mercilessly. What a contrast it is?

More than 72% of our population live below poverty line in this great country of ours. They battle for life everyday. Now we have evolved a plan and seek to implement them touching the needy rural poor directly. I would like to thank the UPA Government for legislating this Employment Guarantee Scheme to benefit the rural poor.

The beneficiaries under this scheme would be getting Rs 6000 per annum by way of getting Rs 60 for 100 days a year. Considering the rise in price index, I wish this minimum wage rate is enhanced soon. I urge upon the Union Government to look into it. If they are to be paid in kind, that is in the form of food grains, then it should be one third of the wages to be paid. 90% of Central funds and 10% of State funds are to be allocated to carry out this scheme. I wish the Centre come forward to bear the entire expense and bear cent percent of expenditure involved in implementing this scheme. I request the hon. Rural Development Minister to look into this and make it a fully funded Central scheme.

My esteemed colleague and fellow member from my neighbouring constituency the hon. Petroleum Minister is present here in this august House now. He knows that our Nagapattinam district did not witness the flawless implementation of ‘Food for Work’ programme conceived as a Centrally funded scheme by the present Union Government. It was not at all implemented satisfactorily. Both of us know how the present State Government in Tamil Nadu mishandled it. We all know the reason. I have recorded this in this august House earlier. 

SGRY, SGSY, IAY, PMGSY, ‘Food for Work’ are all Central schemes aimed at rural poor. Even in the implementation of these poverty alleviation programmes, Central Government’s guidelines were not followed by the State Government in Tamil Nadu now. This accusation of mine has been recorded by me in this august House and we have taken up this with the Union Minister concerned.

This remarkable NREG Scheme must be implemented in all the 200 districts identified to begin with. We would be able to wipe out poverty only when we implement it in all the 600 districts of the country. We must find ways and means for that.

We have evolved monitoring mechanism to oversee the implementation of this programme. I urge upon the Union Government to employ rural youth in those localities as ‘overseers’ of the implementation of these schemes in their local areas. Youth who have passed Class X could be given these jobs. It would generate further job opportunity under this scheme. Lasting employment opportunities to literate/matriculate youth in rural areas can be provided. This suggestion may be seriously considered. The rural youth so employed to monitor the implementation of this scheme can ensure people’s participation, ensure the welfare of the beneficiaries in particular apart from ensuring a livelihood for themselves through a constructive mission taken up in the cause of the nation and its poor. There are certain areas where people come forward to work for even Rs 30 while it is shown on record as Rs 50. We have witnessed such things when similar scheme was implemented in States like Maharashtra. We must bear in mind all our past experiences and must ensure a viable monitoring mechanism. Though the Centre has fixed Rs 60 as the minimum wage under the scheme which in itself needs an upward revision, there are also certain States and regions in the country where people would be ready to work for even Rs 30 per day. It is a hard reality because poverty is so severe in certain rural pockets. I urge upon the Government take note of the severity of poverty.

Sir, the Union Government has announced that we have the right now to get information from the offices of Government. We have Right to Information Act in place. But have we ensured it? I would like to inform the hon. Minister that I wanted to know about the implementation of centrally funded schemes implemented through the State Government in my constituency. Hoping that we have the right to know under the Right to Information Act, I wanted to know about the Central schemes being implemented in Nagai-Thiruvarur districts. Last month I wrote a letter to the District Collectors of those districts about the implementation of Central schemes and their stages and progress commensurate with the fund allocation. A request from a Member of Parliament, a people’s representative from the local area, has not been attended to as yet and the needed information has not been furnished to me as yet. This is how District Collectors respond to a Member of Parliament. So it is imperative that Right to Information Act is implemented with all seriousness it warrants. The District Collectors must be instructed to put up notice boards displaying the details pertaining to the fund allocation, scheme wise allotment, list of beneficiaries under all the schemes area-wise in the districts. Name of projects/schemes, total number of man days, required man power scheme/project wise, list of local village beneficiaries, must be displayed in public places in all the districts all over the country. 

My esteemed colleague Shri P. Mohan noted that the use of machines in carrying out these schemes must be avoided completely. I happily welcome the avoidance of contract system in this scheme.

Nagapattinam district comes under the ambit of this scheme. It must be extended to the neighbouring Tiruvarur district also. 

SOME HON. MEMBERS: Let it be extended to all districts in Tamil Nadu.

SHRI A.K.S. VIJAYAN: I would welcome if all the districts of Tamil Nadu are covered under this scheme to ameliorate poverty in rural areas with dry spell. Instead of 200 districts as indicated now, all the 600 districts must be covered as an ambitious scheme. As far as Tiruvarur, my esteemed colleague hon. Petroleum Minister is well aware that it had severe drought in the last 4 years consecutively. There were at least 20 starvation deaths in Thiruvarur district. Hunger is a problem yet to be wiped out. A seven year old boy named Prakash, Shanmugam a small farmer, Padmavathi an agricultural labour were among those who died due to starvation in the drought conditions. I have repeatedly recorded these starvation deaths in this House. I urge upon the Union Minister to include Thiruvarur district also in the identified districts that would be covered under this scheme. Our colleague Shri Yerran naidu stated that passing of this Bill cannot be construed as a historic one. I would like to point out that it is a scheme to make poverty a history. Father of our nation Mahatma Gandhi said that only when poverty in villages are wiped out nation could attain self sufficiency and prosperity. This historic Bill aims at reaching the poor to help them overcome poverty thereby increasing their productivity to usher in prosperity. There cannot be two different opinions about this Bill that this can ensure social security to the rural poor of this country.

Thanking the Chair again, let me conclude.

SHRI V. KISHORE CHANDRA S. DEO Mr. Chairman, I rise to support this Bill, which we have been discussing now for nearly two days. This is a path-breaking legislation. For the first time, by statute, the Government will be ensuring some kind of employment to provide social security to the poorest people in the country.

Poverty alleviation programmes have been there earlier on. They have been mentioned by many of my colleagues who have spoken from all sides of the House. However, there is a qualitative difference between those programmes and the one which is before the House today. Earlier programmes provided only for an average of 20 days of guarantee. They had no statutory backing and, hence, the legislation which Parliament is going to enact, which this august House is going to enact now, will be a path-breaking law and a historic legislation. This was a commitment that was made by the UPA Government. The Commitment was not to provide jobs for one crore people every year; the commitment that we made was to provide some kind of succour to the poor people in the rural areas of this country.

Mr. Chairman, Sir, economic reforms do not mean betterment of only the business houses or the industrialists. In a country like India, there can be no reforms which do not address the needs of the poor. A majority of our people live in rural areas. There has been migration from rural areas to mega-cities, which has been a pressing problem of recent times. We do hope that in course of time, this will reverse the trend of migration from rural areas to cities. 

Several Members who have spoken have lamented the fact that only 200 districts are being taken up under this Scheme to begin with. This is only a beginning; this is not the end of it. After all, every Government has its constraints. And, a provision which was not there in the original Bill when it was introduced has been incorporated now that within a time-frame of five years, the entire country will be covered by this Scheme. So, it is not as if the Scheme will end with 200 districts. In course of time, certainly, this will spread to different parts of the country. I am sure that with the six to eight per cent growth in our economy that we have been witnessing every year, finances will not be a constraint, as far as this aim is concerned or this end is concerned.

Mr. Chairman, Sir, the Standing Committee in its Report had recommended universal entitlement on a self-targeting basis. Personally, I wish that this Bill gave universal entitlement to every citizen. However, as I said earlier, this is only the beginning. So, the concept of household has also been changed, and every household will be given 100 days of work. I do hope, and the Minister is sitting over here, that in time to come, maybe next year, he will bring an amendment to see that this entitlement becomes universal and self-targeting.

I would just like to point out one or two lacunae in the Bill. This Bill provides for the Panchayati Raj institutions in implementation of works. An amendment was brought to the Seventy-third Amendment to the Constitution: Panchayat Extension to Scheduled Areas. I would just like to quote a certain provision in the new amendment that was brought to the Seventy-third Constitutional Amendment. Section 4 (e) of PESA states:

“Every Gram Sabha shall --

(i) approve of the plans, programmes and projects for social and economic development before such plans, programmes and projects are taken up for implementation by the Panchayat at the village level;

(ii) be responsible for the identification or selection of persons as beneficiaries under the poverty alleviation and other programmes;”

Section 4 (f) states:

“Every Panchayat at the village level shall be required to obtain from the Gram Sabha a certification of utilisation of funds by that Panchayat for the plans, programmes and projects referred to in clause (e[R44] );”

I quoted this Section of the amended Constitution (Seventy-Third Amendment) Act because unless Gram Sabhas are entitled to undertake this job, it will be a violation of the Constitution. It means that the provisions of this Act cannot be implemented in the Scheduled areas. Therefore, I would urge upon the hon. Minister to make a change in sub-sections (1) and (3) of Section 16. I suggest that the words ‘recommendations of’ in those sub-sections may be substituted by the words ‘shelf of projects approved by the Gram Sabha’. If this amendment is made, I believe there may not be any problem to implement the provisions of this scheme in the Scheduled areas of the country.

I would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister to a recommendation made by the Standing Committee. This is at para 2.36A on Page 20 of the report wherein the Committee has strongly recommended that in view of the fact that the Schedule Five and Schedule Six areas in the country are the most backward and people residing there are the poorest, these areas should be included in the first phase of implementation of Employment Guarantee legislation. I would presume that the additional 50 Districts would include such areas as the Standing Committee has recommended unanimously. 

The Standing Committee has given a unanimous report. The report is there with the Government and it will strengthen the hands of the hon. Minister. I would like to appeal to the hon. Minister to utilise the recommendations of the Committee to bring in amendments as and when necessary. For instance, I would certainly like to believe that not very far from now, maybe in the coming year, the Minister would extend this entitlement to everyone to make it universal. I also believe that apart from extending the present facility at this stage to the Scheduled areas, every backward region will be considered in the near future. I am sure that it may not take us even five years to cover the entire country. Let us not be pessimistic about the fact that only 200 Districts have been covered now. A noble beginning has been made. An effort which was never made before is now coming into the Statute Book. I do not see any reason why this is not going to work out.

Mr. Chairman, Sir, I would like to say to the Minister a word about the wage rate. The recommendations which came from various quarters and sources stated that the minimum wage rate that is decided by every State under the Wage Act of 1948 should be taken into consideration. However, there are certain States where the wage rate was much less than the wage rate in certain other States. Therefore, the Standing Committee felt that the minimum wage rate fixed by a State should be taken as the minimum wage rate as long as it is not less than 75 per cent of the national wage rate. This is because this has covered most of the States which have already fixed the minimum wage rate. Now the Government has decided to make a uniform wage of Rs.60. It is all right. Let Rs.60 be the minimum wage. However, I would prefer that those States where higher minimum wages are fixed, those rates should be made applicable as the Bill originally intended it to be.

I would like to appeal to the Minister to ensure that the quality of food grains which are given is good and fit for consumption. Most of the other aspects have been gone into by most of my colleagues and I would not take the time of the House[KMR45] .

But again I would like to repeat that this change which I had recommended has to be taken up. Otherwise, it would be a futile exercise.

SHRI SHRINIWAS DADASAHEB PATIL Sir, I thank you for giving me this opportunity. On behalf of Nationalist Congress Party, I am here to stand and support this Bill. 

‘The National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill’, its name itself, and especially its third Section relating to guarantee of rural employment to poor households, connotes that this is the Bill for rural people. When we are thinking of ‘Bharat Nirman’ and are looking to the welfare of poor people, this scheme means and is meant for the welfare of poor people or poor households from the rural areas. In fact, I am proud and I feel privileged to tell you that, when minimum employment guarantee scheme was pioneered in Maharashtra, I was one of the officers who were implementing that scheme as District Magistrate. I have seen people, after the agricultural operations, without any work and taking money from the local creditors and as such paying huge interest payments. As soon as the harvest was over, they used to be without money. There, the Government thought of giving them employment guarantee. When a hundred or more people came together and applied to the Tehsildar, the Tehsildar was bent to give them the opportunity. But here, in this Bill, there is no necessity of even hundred people coming together. Even if a man, one poor man, applies to the machinery with a request that he should be employed and given an opportunity to sell his labour whether skilled or unskilled, he will be given the opportunity. I welcome this Bill because employment is to be given to a poor household and that too, at the same time, in the rural areas. Provision for providing guaranteed employment is there - one is aware that, under this scheme, he will have work for hundred days at least. The wage rate is also worth mentioning. Minimum wage guarantee is given. So, there is no exploitation of any sort of a labour. Minimum guarantee is given and different areas are to be given different rates of such a minimum wage. Payment of unemployment allowance as such is one of the main features of this Bill[pkp48] . 

ªÉc ÉÊ´É¶Éä­ÉiÉÉ cè <ºÉ ÉÊ¤ÉãÉ àÉå, BÉDªÉÉåÉÊBÉE if he applies for it and if he does not get the opportunity or if he does not get any response from the authorities, then from the date of his application, for at least 15 days, he will be given non-employment allowance. It is to look after the poor household or a poor man or poor people in the rural areas. It will be useful especially when they have nothing to do because when the agricultural operations are over, they are without any work. So, I am here to support this Bill.

In fact, when my leader Shri Sharad Pawar was the Chief Minister of Maharashtra, he implemented one scheme in the area of horticulture. The only thing that a farmer is expected to do is to volunteer his field to be taken over. The plantation was done in those fields; and I will tell you that the fruit bearing trees all over Maharashtra are fetching good prices. So, here my submission would be that the horticulture processing industries should also be brought within the net of this Employment Guarantee Scheme. 

Some of the educated unemployed youth should be promoted to have small processing factories or workshop in rural areas; maybe one workshop or a factory amidst ten villages so that whatever fruits are cultivated – when they are not getting guaranteed prices – they would be brought to the workshop or factory and they would be processed. In fact, this scheme is being implemented to look after each and every individual from the poor family.

May I tell you that women are more likely to be benefited by this scheme? As we have seen, the number of women in doing labour is much more and their final status in the village will be increased because they practically honestly do the work and earn money. 

In Maharashtra, food is also being given to the labour. So, cash payment along with food is being given to the family and he is not to extend his hand for any credit, in a rural area. I support this Bill on behalf of the Nationalist Congress Party. This scheme is very much beneficial for soil conservation efforts, for water conservation measures, for building roads, for construction of earthen dams, etc. Those who want to work will get the work and those who want to get the work done will get good people and honest people to work on the projects. 

Therefore, I congratulate the Government for bringing forward this Bill. I wholeheartedly support this Bill on behalf of my Party. Thank you very much.

We have given so much importance to the Gram Sabhas that it constitutes the foundation of the entire National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill. In this connection, I am obliged to refer to the comments of my colleague, Shri Kishore Chandra Deo, who is not with us at this moment, who asked whether in PESA, in the Fifth Schedule areas covered by the Panchayat (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 provisions – he specifically mentioned 4(3) -- of that Act would be implemented or not. I am afraid Shri Kishore Chandra Deo made a mistake, I apologise for using that word, in saying that the PESA amended the Constitution[snb51] . 

It did not. It fulfilled the Constitutional requirement. The Constitution directs that Parliament shall, for Fifth Schedule Areas, prepare an Act which covers the extension of these provisions to those scheduled areas. In pursuance of that, the 1996 Act was passed by this Parliament and it has gone to the States. It is for the States to enact their laws in accordance with the PESA. This involved, very often, an amendment of their extant Panchayati Raj Acts. 

Now, if in some States this is not being done, the concerns expressed by Shri Kishore Chandra Deo should be addressed to that State Government and not to this Parliament. I certainly hope that in all States of India, which have Fifth Schedule Areas, the letter and the spirit of PESA will be fully respected. If it is so, then automatically, the concerns that he has expressed with reference to this Bill will also be met. In these circumstances, we now come to the gram panchayat.

SHRI SURESH PRABHAKAR PRABHU : Mr. Chairman, Sir, the hon. Minister mentioned a very important point. He said that clause 13 of the proposed Bill gives unqualified powers to the panchayats and, therefore, the point raised by Shri Kalyan Singh will not apply. If you read clause 13, – Shri Mani Shankar Aiyar can read it – clause 13 (1) says:

“The Panchayat at district level in every district within which a Scheme is being implemented shall constitute a Standing Committee consisting of such number of its members and subject to such terms and conditions as may be prescribed by the State Government to supervise, monitor and oversee the implementation of the Scheme within the district.”

Therefore, it is not an unqualified power that is given to the panchayat. It can vary from State to State. The State Government can decide as to what should be the powers of supervision of that Standing Committee which is going to be constituted under clause 13. Therefore, if the spirit with which he is saying that is to be taken to the logical conclusion, then what we really need to do is to take away the powers from the State Government, to change from one State to another State the power of the respective Standing Committee which actually is going to exercise the power that he talked about.

SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: Sir, it would be undesirable to give unfettered powers to any institution in our democracy. Democracy functions best when there are checks and balances.

SHRI BIKRAM KESHARI DEO Mr. Chairman, Sir, if the hon. Minister yields I would like to seek a clarification.

SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: Let me finish. I do not yield. I will give you a chance after I finish.

Sir, it is precisely to check the unfettered powers of any element of the system that these checks and balances have been built in. I do not believe that it would be constitutional for us here to prescribe a uniform model for all the State Governments because the State List in the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution clearly puts the responsibility for Panchayati Raj on the State Governments and what we have to always perform is a delicate constitutional balancing act between the advocacy role of the Centre and the constitutional responsibilities that have been entrusted to the States. If one sees that any given State Government is violating either the letter of the Constitution or the law or, more importantly, the spirit in which that law has been prepared, then it is the job of the Union Ministry of Panchayati Raj to go there and arrive at a conclusion by a process of cajoling, begging, persuading and at some times, perhaps, with a little bit of threatening.

Sir, it has been my experience in the last year that if you get together the representatives of the State Governments, there is total unanimity, not just consensus; 150 action points have been agreed by all of us sitting together in a period of just 150 days last year. Now I am undertaking tours of the States and I find that it is very easy to be able to arrive, by consensus with them, at the important steps that need to be taken to improve things in any given State.

So, with trust in our constitutional order, a constitutional order which gives responsibilities to the panchayats within a framework where the State Governments have an overall responsibility to the people through their State Legislatures and which gives certain responsibilities to the Centre to be responsible to the same people of India through this august House, the Parliament of India, I think, we need to move forward. We are moving forward. This is truly a historic Bill, because for the first time unambiguously the Panchayati Raj Institutions, the Gram Sabhas and Ward Sabhas which support these Institutions, have been given full recognition, full devolution of powers and full respect.

SHRI SURESH PRABHAKAR PRABHU Sir, we are about to pass a very important legislation. India is a country, which should not be proud of the fact that we have the highest number of people living below poverty line. I sometimes wonder, if those people were to live in a separate country, that would be the poorest country in the world, with the second largest population in the world. 

17.31 hrs (Shri Devendra Prasad Yadav in the Chair)

So many poor people are living in a country like India and therefore, when we are addressing the concern of such poor people by way of a legislation, this is a welcome step. While doing that we must be sure that the object, which has been stated in the object clause of this particular legislation, is really reflected in the substantive position of the legislation.

Sir, why we are talking about it and why I justify this because the only way of survival for poor is his ability to work. He has no asset and therefore, no resort to using his capital for earning income. Therefore, the only way he can earn income is by working. Therefore, when we are actually guaranteeing a right to work, it is something which was not even stated in the Constitution, it is something which is definitely welcome. While we are doing that, we must be absolutely sure that we are actually doing what we really need to do.

Sir, we are talking about livelihood security for the poorest of the poor in the country. When we talk about livelihood security, can you believe that those people, who are going to work for 100 days in a year earning less than the minimum wage, which is stipulated – I will come to that point later – save something which will help them to earn income for the remaining 265 days in a year? When you earn for 100 days, you need to also survive for the remaining 265 days. Therefore, if you are providing livelihood security, which is really required, then in that case, it is not sufficient to say that we will provide you guarantee for only 100 days and for remaining 265 days, how you will survive is not my concern. Therefore, if you are providing livelihood security, which is the basic object of the Bill, as has been stated in the object clause, in that case it is not enough that we can give for 100 days, it must be given round the year, for 365 days of the year and that too at the minimum wage and not below that. It is because the minimum  wage is the wage which is calculated under the Act passed by this Parliament on the basis of the minimum amount of money required for a person to survive. On this basis the minimum wage is calculated. So, how can you pay anything which is lower than the minimum wage? It is a violation of the Act passed by this Parliament itself. Therefore, I personally feel, that the clause 100 days should be removed and it should be round the year and the amount should not be Rs. 60 per day, but minimum wage.

Sir, when we are talking of livelihood security, the other important issue is that when we are going to give a minimum wage, if at all we do that, even the State Government is unable to provide jobs. In that case, the amount of money that will be entitled for that poor person is only 25 per cent of the minimum wage. 

Now, when we are talking of livelihood security, do you mean to say that the State Government finds it easier not to provide a wage and 25 per cent of the wage will be paid? Do you think he will be able to survive? So, if you are talking of livelihood security, it is not enough to say that we will provide only 100 days wage and not even minimum wage and that too after assuring that to say that if the Government is not willing to provide it, we will give only 25 per cent of that. Therefore, this goes against the spirit for which we are discussing this. Therefore, I really request that that should be done.

Sir, I am talking of minimum wages, minimum employment, so give me minimum time please.

Sir, why is this really done and why only in 150 districts? I am really worried that they will do it for 150 districts out of 600 plus districts of the country. Many people will migrate from one place to another. But then there is a clause saying that if a person goes from one village to another, unless he resides in the vicinity of that village, he will not be entitled to draw wages. Just imagine, some workers, some poor people want to migrate from an adjoining district, which is not identified as a poor district, to get a job will not get a job. How is it going to work? Therefore, I also feel that this provision also needs to be properly amended while doing this.

Sir, the other issue is a very important issue and I hope my friends from the Left will sympathise with this. We are told that of the 100 days in a year, he will get a job only six days in the seven days’ week[r55] .

Do you mean to say that on the seventh day, he is not going to get paid? It is what is required. When they talk about Schedule 2 of this Bill that there are going to be a number of labour-friendly incentives like providing fresh drinking water, medical facilities, why not seven days’ wage also should be paid having a person worked for six days? It is because that is what is normally done. Therefore, this again is required to be introduced and incorporated. Therefore, I feel that this needs to be done.

SHRI SURESH PRABHAKAR PRABHU : Before we start the programme, I hope we take certain precautions. One of the precautions that we need to take is this. Now, there are only identity cards which are going to be issued but a wage register should also be registered properly. SHRI KHARABELA SWAIN Sir, our Party is not opposed to this Bill specifically when the Standing Committee of Rural Development has in its recommendations described this Bill as a path-breaking piece of legislation brought forward by the Government of India. Shri Kalyan Singh, who has initiated this debate, has chaired the Standing Committee on Rural Development. Shri Kalyan Singh has already mentioned in detail about the lacunae that this Bill is having. I shall not repeat those. The only thing, along with him, I shall mention right from the beginning is this. I urge upon the Government to implement this Bill all over the country including the urban areas within the next two years and also to open this Bill for anybody who wishes to take up such manual job. It should not be confined to any one person in the family. 

Sir, it seems that the UPA Government has set all its hope and expectation on this Bill since it could turn out to be the only tangible achievement of this Government. This desperate hope was the hallmark of the maiden speech made by Madam Sonia Gandhi in the Fourteenth Lok Sabha, ably followed by a highly politically-oriented speech made by the hon. Member, Shri Jyotiraditya M. Scindia, who among themselves claimed about ten times that this National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill is the brainchild of the Congress Party. There was a total hesitation on their part to cede any credit to any other party including their colleagues in the Left. Naturally, at the end of the speech, there was very reluctant thumping of desk by the Members belonging to the Left Parties. 

I have no quarrel with the Congress Party. Let them appropriate all the credit; if this Bill succeeds. It is all their credit and I wish them the best. You may call me a pessimist, you may call me a cynic and you may call me a person having a negative mentality but, as a Member of the Opposition, I think, it is my bounden duty to bring it to the notice of this Government as to where lies the bottleneck and what could throttle such a scheme from eradicating poverty.

Sir, take the example of the Maharashtra Bill, which is the pre-cursor of this National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill. My basic question is this. This Bill is going to put the exchequer under tremendous pressure. But will it bring in compensatory spin-off in the form of reduced poverty level? 

I will just quote the recommendations of the Standing Committee on Rural Development. It says, in page 7, about the failures of the Scheme in Maharashtra. I shall go one by one. It says:

“The programme still continues after 30 years without any decline in the demand for unskilled wage work under the scheme. ”

Does it mean that after 30 years nothing has happened in Maharashtra and still people are going for unskilled work[lh57] ?

That clearly means there is a lot of pilferage in this project. The second one is, ‘there has been modest impact in poverty reduction or in unemployment reduction in the State’. There has been a very, very modest reduction. The third one is, ‘the distressed seasonal migration of workers from backward region continues as the guarantee is not really implemented in many cases’. You will understand that it has not done anything with the migration of the labour. And the last one is very important. ‘The quality of the assets created and their maintenance are frequently not satisfactory’. That means the quality of the sustainable assets, the creation of the durable assets, which is the main purpose of the Bill, has failed in Maharashtra even though it has been implemented for the last 31 years. 

You see, why this has happened. Now, let us see page 39. It has been given in the Bill what are the schemes, what are the projects that would be taken up. They are, water conservation and water harvesting, drought-proofing, irrigation canals, provision of irrigation facility, land development, renovation of traditional water bodies, flood control and rural connectivity to provide with all weather access. There are works like this. Mostly, these are all earth-related works. We know and all the Members of this House know that when most of our Party members and contractors come to us and demand that they should be given some work, what do they want? They want this kachcha work of laying the kachcha road and digging the pond. Why? It is because the pilferage is the highest there. The officers take the highest percentage in these cases. That is the position. I am very scared that this might happen in this case because this is not going to create any durable asset. It is only going to create some kachcha assets. 

Now, I will come to another point. I will simply give another example. This is The Indian Express. I will give you this as a proof. This is The Indian Express of August 18. It says, “Lesson for Delhi is here. Maharashtra stops work in Solahpur. District Collector signature forged. Musters manipulated by the Government staff. Only in one district, there has been a pilferage of Rs.9.1 crore.” This is the result. This is what happened in Maharashtra. This is from The Indian Express of August 18th. 

So, this is my point. Is this Bill not going to open the floodgate of corruption? That is my apprehension. This is a very sincere apprehension, and I gave you the example. … (Interruptions)

SHRI KHARABELA SWAIN : This is my actual question. Actually how many people are going to come for that work? Let me tell you I am having a printing press in my State. I want a person who is a machine operator who is to be trained. I have been giving advertisements through newspapers, including through my newspaper. I am telling many people that I want a person to whom I am prepared to pay Rs.1,500 per month. But for the last six months nobody is coming for work. Even if anybody is coming for work, he is quitting the job after 10 days. It is only because he thinks that Rs.1,500 per month is a pittance; it is a very small amount. You are going to give Rs.60 per day. That means, it would come to Rs.6,000 for 100 days in a year. That means, it is Rs.500 per month. When you are going to give Rs.60 per day, I do not know how many people will come forward. I am asking a very simple question. Are the educated people of this country very interested in a salary of Rs.500, a pittance, per month? They want white-collar jobs. I am very doubtful whether many people will come forward. In a State like Kerala, the minimum wage is Rs.130. If you say you will give Rs.60, who is going to come forward to take up this job when more wage on daily basis is available outside? So, that is my doubt[m58] .  

There are two aspects relating to poverty: one is absolute poverty and the other is relative poverty. Absolute poverty refers to the number of people or proportion of population below the poverty line. Relative poverty is exactly the story you narrated several times in this House. You were describing the other day the difference between the poor and the rich. You said that while the poor man was walking on the street the rich man was climbing on an elephant; thus, there was a difference of 10-12 feet. Now, the rich people are flying by aircraft at a height of 30,000 feet. This is relative poverty and these are our poverty dimensions.

During the early decades after Independence, the levels of income were low and the GDP growth was meagre. Consequently, poverty levels were too high, both in terms of proportions and absolute numbers but relative poverty and income disparity were virtually low. Since the mid-1980s, there was economic acceleration of about six per cent per year and poverty declined but the relative poverty has increased. Now, the major problem before this Government is how to eradicate this relative poverty so that poverty would go away altogether.

Let us take the example of Telengana. In Telengana, there is a Naxalite movement because they say the level of poverty is very high. I had gone to Telengana. If you compare Telengana with the prosperous areas of Orissa, I think, Telengana would fare much better than the prosperous areas of Orissa. I come from these more prosperous areas that they are worse than Telengana. This is not absolute poverty. This is relative poverty because the people of Telengana think that the people of coastal Andhra Pradesh are rich. If they come to Orissa, they would actually know how poor Orissa is. That is why, I say, it is a question of mindset and it should be done away with. The Government should carefully design the economic growth strategy. We should aim at reducing the imbalances between States, between rural and urban areas, and among various social groups. During the time of the NDA Government, the Government had created infrastructure that aimed at removing relative poverty but the UPA Government is rather more interested in removing absolute poverty, which has actually come down during the last two decades.

Another point relates to the quality of work. I have carefully gone through the recommendations of the Standing Committee. Many experts have appeared before the Standing Committee and given their opinion. The opinion of the experts was that the Government never talked about the quality of work. The experts simply wanted that we should relax all the work norms. Actually they want a relaxation of work norms. There was a provision that people should work diligently for seven hours. The Government wants to remove it. They say: “There is no question of diligence. He would just do whatever work he wants.” If there were five women, one woman among them would be a babysitter. So, out of five women, only four women would work. For pregnant women, there is also a provision that three months’ wages would be paid without any work. There would be separate types of work for the handicapped and disabled persons. Can we not directly help those pregnant women and disabled persons? Why should this be done in the name of Employment Guarantee Scheme? Are we not keeping more loopholes in this bill by leaving room for discretion so that the officials would get excuses to resort to corrupt practices[e59] ?

Hon. Minister, Shri Mani Shankar Aiyar, was telling about the muster roll. In the EGS scheme which was implemented earlier, there was also a provision for a muster roll. You come to our village and you will find that there is no muster roll anywhere. 

I am putting the question to the Government. The hon. Minister is present here. Does the Government feel that the good quality of irrigation project should actually be done through manual work? I do not think that good quality of irrigation work could be taken up through manual work. It is because, if you dig the canal, you dig the canal and you put it on the bank and with one shower of water everything will just come to the canal and again it will be silted. Actually, this happens and this is my experience and this is also your experience. 

I am putting another question. This Government has made this Bill a legal entity. Now, I have an apprehension that many people will go to the court. Some of them also maybe politically motivated. Now, what are you going to do about it? How many cases will you fight? It is because some people will say, `I asked for job and the Government did not give it to me.’ 

Now, I would just like to read what the Times of India has said. It cannot be said that it is an Opposition-oriented newspaper. I quote:

“The Group of Ministers has given a go-by to `fiscal prudence’, in pursuing an expensive and potentially `highly wasteful’ national programme of political expediency. The Finance Ministry raised a `Fiscal Defence Wall’ against the Bill. Fiscal experts within the Government are aghast that it is not the usual suspect – the Left, but the Congress Chief who is attempting to endear herself to the `aam admi’ at the risk of leading the Government to financial ruin. Even if the States foot a part of the bill, the costs are likely to be prohibitive for the Centre.”

These are the comments given by the newspaper. Under no stretch of imagination you can tell that it is the `Opposition’ newspaper. 

The hon. Minister for Water Resources, Shri Priyaranjan Dasmunsi, was telling that because of the great nationalisation and because of the pro-poor effect of the late Shrimati Indira Gandhi Government, the fate of the poor had changed. I will just give you one example. During 1991, Shri Chandra Shekhar was the Prime Minister for only four months. He had to pledge gold for bringing some foreign exchange reserves. Why did it happen? Did he commit so much of a mistake that within four months he had to pledge gold? It was because of the economic mismanagement from 1980 to 1990 that we had to suffer. I apprehend that this is exactly going to happen now. 

My last point is about removing the relative poverty. The first thing is that more money should be put to make the people literate. It is the education which will ultimately remove poverty.  The Government should put more money in the rural infrastructure like road, power, health and irrigation and not in the name of Employment Guarantee Scheme. You put the money and people will get the opportunity to stand on their own legs and to generate work on their own. If that is not done, then I have an apprehension that in a State like West Bengal, the entire money will be appropriated by the Comrades and by the Cadre.

Thank you very much.

PROF. M. RAMADASS : Sir, we welcome this Bill because this is in consonance with the policy of our Party – PMK. This intends to ensure full employment to all able-bodied persons in the country. Our policy is to provide education to all and jobs to all and, therefore, this National Rural Employment 

*Not Recorded

Guarantee Bill provides for the achievement of this objective. Therefore, we appreciate and congratulate the hon. Minister for Rural development. I think he will go into the annals of India’s economic history by bringing this radical, rather a revolutionary Bill which will go to wipe out the tears of Indian eyes. 

In 1947, when we got Independence, Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru said : “The objective of India’s Independence is to wipe out every tear from every Indian eye”. That may be beyond us. But as long as there are tears, our work will not be over. I find that this Bill is designed to achieve that long-eluding goal of Government of India and also of Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru. 

Our friend on the other side, Shri Kharabela Swain, was talking like an economist and saying that this will not reduce the relative poverty and that the relative poverty is increasing. If he had read a little amount of Economics, he would have known that this Bill is intended to a targeted group who are actually unemployed and who do not have any income and hence the purchasing power[krr61] . 

Therefore, among the two unequals, this Bill tries to address those people who do not get employment. So, this is going to address the people who will get some income and therefore, the gap between the absolute poverty and the relative poverty will be reduced by the introduction of this Bill. Perhaps, if there is a nation-wide application of the Bill, that may contribute to widening of the gap, but this Bill for rural areas will bridge the gap between the relative poverty and the absolute poverty. 

He was also mentioning about The Times of India according to which the fiscal experts in the Finance Ministry are alarmed about the cost. The cost of implementing this programme for this year would be only Rs. 13,000 crore which can be easily funded by the Finance Ministry without increasing the fiscal deficit or the revenue deficit of the Government, but with regard to the benefit of the scheme to the people. I should mention that 150 million rural households in this country will have bread-winners, after the passage of this Bill. 

We will have to look at this Bill from the background in which this Bill has been piloted. When I read this Bill, I was reminded of the statement of one of the greatest economists of the 20th Century, Lord John Maynard Keynes who had said:

“The outstanding faults of the economic society in which we live are its failure to provide for full employment and its arbitrary and inequitable distribution of wealth and income … ”

What he had said in 1936 holds good for India even today. 

The two major problems that we are facing today are unemployment and poverty. Unemployment and poverty are the two sides of the same coin. If a person does not get any job, he does not have any income and if he does not have income, he does not have consumption. Therefore, either from the consumption point of view or from the income point of view, you cannot eradicate poverty unless people get income as well as employment. This Bill precisely provides for it. It may be true that the past experiences have failed, but the past experiences' failures need not be a lesson for the failure of the future also. 

There are a number of innovative features in this Bill which would try to ensure greater employment opportunities to the people in this country. He said that the relative poverty is increasing. Yes, the relative poverty has been increasing, but it has been increasing because his NDA Government was pursuing relentlessly the economic reforms without a human face. Economic reforms that had been initiated during the last six years have created a path of jobless growth, a path of human-faceless growth, what we call a nihilistic development. When we allow these economic reforms to take the country forward, it will not automatically generate employment opportunities. That is why, Madam Sonia Gandhi while participating in the discussion on the Bill said that 'I believe that we cannot just sit idle and hope that economic reforms alone will create adequate employment opportunities in rural India'. This is true.

When you look at the evidences that are coming out of the economic reforms, we have seen a marginalisation process where the big industries are swallowing the medium industries, medium industries are swallowing the small-scale industries and small-scale industries are taking away cottage industries. As a result, we have produced only unemployment in the country, even among the unskilled labourers. Therefore, if these unskilled labourers are to be taken care of, who are in greater majority, we have to make specific provision for the employment opportunities and this Bill, for the first time, recognises this faulty planning process in this country and tries to give a boost to the bottom up approach to development. Therefore, it will provide a lot of employment opportunities. 

Many of the deficiencies he has mentioned, like it will lead to corruption, it will not bring about qualitative work etc., are all taken care of by the Bill. If you look into the various components of the Bill, you will be able to understand that there is a greater amount of monitoring of the scheme at every level. There is a transparency and there is accountability. There is vigilance on the part of the people who are involved in this scheme. Therefore, all the past mistakes associated with the Maharashtra Bill or the Rural Landless Employment Guarantee Bill or the Employment Assurance Scheme, which we have implemented in the past, will not be committed or will not be repeated in this scheme because there are built-in mechanisms where there will be greater vigilance in evolution of the scheme, at every level. Therefore, given theses superior salient features of the Bill, I hope that this Bill will be able to tackle the basic issues of unemployment and poverty in the country. One of the important salient features of the Bill is that this is a need-based programme. Perhaps there are only very few programmes in the country which are need-based[reporter62] .

What is a need-based programme? It would provide employment to those who are in need of it. This Bill does not say that all of you come and get the job. Those who want the job are registered, and they can apply to get a job. This would also be need-based because it would help to create the assets needed by the society, as the labour power is not going to be wasted. The labour power of this country is going to be used for conversion of manpower into real assets. Therefore, all the assets or infrastructure that are required by the society would be created with the help of employment, to be given through this programme. On the one hand we would be creating assets needed by the society, and on the other, we would be using the labour power required for the society. 

Therefore, the entire programme is a need-based one. At the time of its implementation, namely, when the people get employment and income, and purchasing power, consumption and the demand for goods and services would increase. As a result of this, the industrial production and agricultural production would increase, and it would result in higher growth rate in the economy to rise. We are already reaching a stage of seven per cent growth rate in the economy, and the provision of employment opportunities would increase the growth rate. 

If this growth rate is sustained, then we would be able to follow the path of social justice, and growth in the economy. This is the same point that our Hon. Prime Minister made during his Independence Day address. He aptly said that if we sustain this pace between seven and eight per cent growth, then in the next five years to 10 years we would be able to wipe out poverty in the country.

MR. CHAIRMAN: Mr. Ramadass, please conclude your speech.

PROF. M. RAMADASS : This would no longer be a dream, but it would become a possibility now. Eradication of poverty has been a dream so far, but it is going to be a possibility now. I am saying this because by providing employment opportunities we are actually going to accelerate the growth or development or the tempo of development, which would wipe out poverty. It has now become a possibility, and it has become a possibility because of the introduction of this Bill. Therefore, this Bill has got a long term objective, and we will have to appreciate the Government for bringing this Bill.

One Hon. Member asked a question : Have the State Governments been consulted on this Bill? Have the State Governments agreed to implement this Bill? The answer is yes. There is greater co-operation and greater co-ordination between the Centre and the States as far as this Bill is concerned. I am also aware of the fact that the Hon. Rural Development Minister has sent the draft Bill to all the States twice on this issue. Their comments on this Bill were received, and those comments have been incorporated in this Bill. This Bill has come before us in this form today after going to the Standing Committee also. 

All the State Governments have agreed to share 10 per cent of the total funds, and 90 per cent of the funds would be borne by the Central Government. The Central Government has also agreed that it will make advance payment of the quarterly money every time, so that the State Governments would not feel reluctant to spend the money. Therefore, by involving the States and involving the Panchayati Raj, the Government is now bringing a real, true devolution of powers from top to the bottom. It is in real terms grass-root democracy taking a greater and vibrant shape in this country, and this Bill provides for it.

MR. CHAIRMAN: Mr. Ramadass, please conclude your speech.

PROF. M. RAMADASS : Sir, having said this, I would also like to draw the attention of the hon. Rural Development Minister to one or two lapses in the Bill, which I hope the Chairman would be able to identify. I am a professor of economics. Therefore, I should be given grace of speaking on some of the technical points of this Bill. Sir, I am sure that you would be able to give me some more time for it.

I would now like to talk about some of the inconsistencies in the Bill. I would like to satisfy the other camp also by pointing out the deficiencies in this Bill. One of the important points is this. In the first paragraph of the Bill it is said that : 

“…wage employment in every financial year to every household… ”

But in the very next page, namely, in Chapter II it is stated :

“…provide to every poor household …”

What does it mean? In the earlier page, the word ‘poor household’ is removed. I find this inconsistency here, and I want to make a comment about it. Have you made BPL census survey to decide about poor household? Are they available at the level of the States? I know that the Supreme Court has intervened in this matter, and your Department has already written to various State Governments asking them not to finalise the census reports on poverty line. How did you draw the poverty line? Have you taken income as the basis for it or consumption as the basis for it or the various indicators on poverty[ak63] ? 

Now, if that has been taken into account it is right. When the BPL Census is not available, how are you going to implement the Scheme immediately by drawing the people from below the poverty-level households? That is one thing.

Secondly, the Bill mentions that an adult means, “a person who is 18 years of age”. I would feel that instead of merely saying ‘an adult’, you must say, ‘an unemployed adult’. Supposing a boy of 18 years of age going to college may enter into a kind of collusion with the programme officer and say, “Sir, I will go to the college in the evening, but give me a job in the morning. If you do not provide a job, you give me half of the unemployment allowance.” Will it not lead to a situation where people who are not willing to work also get enrolled in this? Therefore, we should clearly say that if there is a college going boy, he will be treated as an employed boy and not an unemployed boy. We have to clearly say that.

I have two more points to make. Coming to the payment of unemployment allowance, the Bill says that if a person is not to get a job within 15 days, then for the first 30 days, you are going to give him only one-fourth of the minimum wage; and for the remaining 70 days, you are going to give him half of it. Why is this distinction? When the Government is not able to find a job for a person within 15 days of his enrolment, he is going to remain unemployed, whether it is for 30 days or 100 days. You should give him Rs. 30 because you are going to give only Rs. 60, if he works. Why do you distinguish between 30 days and 70 days? You must make it that half of the wages will be given as unemployment allowance, and you must provide jobs for all those who are registering. 

When you look at the monitoring mechanism, there is definitely a fault in the composition of the Central Council. The functions of the Central Council with regard to implementation of the scheme will be more of technical in nature. They will have to evolve, formulate and implement the schemes and monitor them. All these aspects are technical tasks. Have you provided for any technical expert in the composition of this Council? 

Who are going to be consultants for this project? The Bill says that there will be a chairperson. It is not mentioned whether he will be an Economist or not. Nowhere, the Bill has mentioned or provided for an expert. I would urge upon the Government to specifically mention that some economist or statistician or sociologist will be involved in the Central Council.

When we come to section 10, Sl. No. 30, the Bill says that, “Provided also that not less than one-third of the non-official members shall be belonging to the Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and minorities.” They are going to be there in the Council as Members. Why do you not include ‘Other Backward Classes”? Therefore, I would suggest that OBCs should be included in both the State Councils and in the Central Council.

There is no scope for management information system in the Bill. Throughout the country, there should be a uniform proforma; there should be a uniform computer software, and all kinds of instructions must be uniform. Therefore, you must create a management information system for the effective implementation of this Scheme.

The District Planning Coordinator is going to play an important role. You say that the Collector may be the Coordinator. A Collector cannot be the Coordinator or the Chairperson for everything. Just look at the workload he has. He will not be able to do the work under this Bill and they do not have the technical background also. Therefore, I urge, this is a very important point that you should note, that a large number of officers belonging to the Indian Economic Service and the Indian Statistical Service, who are located in Delhi, should be sent to all the districts to look after this programme, including DRDA programmes, and the econimic administration should be left in their hands only. 

Then, the Bill mentions about a labour budget. I feel that the labour budget takes into account only the demand for labour and not the supply of labour. Supply is not mentioned. I feel that before you commence the scheme, you should try to prepare an output budget. That is what the thinking of the Government of India today is[R64] .

What is that output budget? Before you take up a scheme, you should state as to how many days of employment is going to be created, how many people are going to be employed, what are the assets that you are going to create, etc. If you prepare that kind of an output budget, it will be possible for you to monitor the scheme and bring the benefits of the scheme to the people. 

18.20 hrs. (Shri Varkala Radhakrishnan in the Chair) 

I would agree that all works mentioned in Schedule-I are important. In addition to them several other works in the rural areas should also be included. You must take up community sanitary latrines. The Hon’ble Minister has already written a letter to all the MLAs in the country stating that the condition of sanitary work is awfully bad in the rural areas and that it should be taken up. But the Bill does not include that. So, we must be able to take up the work of community latrines, houses for SCs and STs, community centres, etc. In fact, all the works that have been mentioned in the MPLAD Scheme should also be entrusted to those people who are coming under the purview of this Bill. School buildings should also be taken up. Solid waste management works should also be taken up. 

More important than all this is the maintenance. The buildings that have been built, the assets that have been created, the schools that have been constructed, the hospitals that have been created are not properly taken care of. Therefore, they are dying without maintenance. 

MR. CHAIRMAN : Prof. Ramadass, please conclude now. Your time is over. 

PROF. M. RAMADASS : You should create proper supervisory staff.

MR. CHAIRMAN: Please address the chair. Why do you address the Minister?

PROF. M. RAMADASS : Through you, Mr. Chairman, Sir, I would like to mention only two points to the hon. Minister. 

The National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill involves mammoth work, gigantic work. It cannot succeed unless proper, motivated, dedicated, supervisory staff is provided. Unfortunately, this Bill does not provide for it except to make a peripheral mention that some administrative staff would be given to the District Officer. 

This is a landmark Bill. Everybody should accept it. Let us make a beginning. Let us address this issue in a very serious way at the all India level. As the Opposition parties have said, we will have to take into account the urban unemployment also and an all India Bill should come in future. 

Finally, there is no benefit provided for my Union Territory Pondicherry in this Bill. It has been completely left out. District Karaikal of Pondicherry is as backward as any of the most backward Districts in the country. I would urge upon the Hon. Minister to include District Karaikkal as the 201st District in the country under this Bill.

MR. CHAIRMAN: Hon. Members are hereby informed that not more than five minutes will be allowed hereafter.
