SHRI ARJUN SETHI Thank you Mr. Chairman for giving me this opportunity to participate in the discussion on this Bill which is under discussion since Friday. 

Sir, much euphoria has been generated, both inside this House and outside, that with the introduction of this Bill it is hoped that this will be a panacea for all the ills that are prevailing in rural India. But, I must say, this won’t solve the problems but, on the other hand, will create problems.

Sir, since I have very less time available at my disposal, I straightway would ask a few clarifications. First of all, I would like to know this. In my constituency, there is a Scheduled Area named Nilgiri. Under the Fifth Schedule of the Constitution, this area has been declared as a Scheduled Area but the District in which it is included is a forward area. That District has not been identified as a backward District and has not even been included in the National Food for Work Programme. So, what will be the fate of this particular Scheduled Area, that is, Nilgiri in my constituency in the State of Orissa? If that District is not selected for undertaking this kind of national rural employment guarantee programme, then this particular Scheduled Area, that is, Nilgiri, which is a part of Balasore District, may be debarred from getting all the facilities under this particular scheme. If it is debarred, certainly a Constitutional impropriety will be committed. So, I would like to know from this hon. Minister – unfortunately he is not here but his deputy is here - and have clarification on this point. 

Sir, another thing is this. The 200 Districts have not yet been identified. It is declared in this particular Bill that this employment guarantee programme will be spread over in 200 Districts of the country[pkp67] . 

What will be the criteria for selection of these districts? The BPL norm has already been done away with in this Bill and what will be the criteria in that case?

As I have stated earlier, the contiguous districts are Keonjhar and Mayurbhanj in Orissa. These two districts have been included in the National Food for Work Programme. I wish that these two districts might be included in the National Rural Employment Guarantee Programme also. If they are included, how the district of Balasore will not be included in this particular Programme? 

Another thing is this. As has been mentioned, the Bill has intended that whenever there are 50 or more labourers or workers, this particular programme will be implemented. Why is there rigidity about this number 50? Why should that not be relaxed, as has been mentioned by many speakers from this side and from that side of the House? Why is this number 50 very much sacrosanct with the Government? This should be relaxed and it should not be definite. It could be less than 50 also. Whenever there will be a commitment for work by the labourers or by the people living in a particular area, this Programme should be implemented. 

It has also been stated that the wage will be as per the Minimum Wages Act. It differs from State to State. There may be a situation where in a particular district, this particular Programme may be implemented and it may not be implemented in the contiguous districts. This particular Programme may be implemented in a particular district and in the contiguous districts, this Programme may not be implemented, but still SGRY, Rural Landless Employment Programme and such other Programmes may be still in force or may be still implemented or carried out. Then, you may just imagine the fate of these programmes in the contiguous districts. In the district, where the Rural Employment Guarantee Programme is implemented, the rate of wage will be Rs.60 per day and in the next contiguous districts, the rate may be Rs.50. If that were the case, what will be the fate of the Programmes? Wherever there is a higher wage available for the workers, certainly they would like to go to those areas. Then, certainly the other Programmes which are being implemented still in different parts of the country will be the casualty. These are the ambiguities which are very much prevalent in this particular Bill. These ambiguities should be removed; otherwise there will certainly be a lot of confusion. Instead of extending a helping hand to the poor and to the deserving people, there will be confusion and the other Programmes which are still being implemented, will certainly be a casualty[R68] . 

I would not like to repeat all that has been said earlier but would like to ask as to how much amount will be made available to each district. Sir, the Minister has not yet specified the amount to be made available to each district.… (Interruptions)

SHRI PAWAN KUMAR BANSAL : That provision is never made in the Act.

SHRI ARJUN SETHI : At the State or the District level you have the monitoring Committees but it has not been specified as to within what time they are supposed to give their action plans to the district. These are some of the questions which arise in our mind. I admit that this is a very good measure. There is no doubt about it but at the same time these queries must be replied to so that this programme is really helpful to the people.

I once again would like to draw the attention of the hon. Minister – as I have stated earlier also – to the fact that one part of the Balasore district in Orissa State has been declared as Scheduled area and the other part as forward area. How will this particular Scheduled area get support under this programme? You may please clarify this. With these words I thank you.

DR. CHINTA MOHAN I thank Dr. Raghuvansh Prasad Singh for piloting this Bill. While piloting the Bill, he spoke at length and everybody appreciated him. This Bill, which he has introduced, is a very historic Bill and politically it is a very important Bill. I would like to touch only the political part of this Bill. I do not want to go into the technicalities of this Bill.

The UPA Government is a very historic Government. After 57 years of Independence, two ideologically different Parties - the Left Parties and the Congress Party – who were trying to have the supremacy came together to form the Government with the help of other friends. That is why this Government has become a very historic Government. The UPA Government brought a Common Minimum Programme. The theme of this CMP is to give health, education and livelihood to the people. At that time, while forming the Government this entire Common Minimum Programme was prepared by some Professors in the Jawahar Lal Nehru University in a hurry. 

Before speaking about the Bill, I would like to quote a Resolution passed by the Communist Party (M) in February 2002 in Hyderabad. This Government formed today just because of the February 2002 Resolution of the CPM passed in their plenary Congress at Hyderabad. It was a very important Resolution in the Indian political history and I quote:

“CPM will support Congress to defeat BJP. ”

This is a very important decision. This Resolution was passed in February 2002 in the CPM Congress held at Hyderabad and because of this Resolution today the UPA Government is formed. We all are aware that the Congress and the Left Parties had ideological differences[R69] .

Though they fought with each other for more than five decades to have a political supremacy yet for a cause – to have a secular Government at the Centre – this Government was formed. I congratulate the leaders who brought that resolution in February 2002. I bow my head before that resolution and the comrades who passed that resolution. It is because of that resolution we could form the Government and our hon. Minister who is sitting here could pilot this Bill. I also congratulate Shrimati Sonia Gandhi, the Chairperson of UPA who is my Leader. While speaking the other day on this Bill, she said that it is a very historic Bill. Really, it is a historic Bill and politically also it is a very important Bill. 

I wanted to tell how this UPA Government was formed. For the benefit of this House, I would like to say that in April 1999, Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee got up as the Prime Minister and sat as Ex Prime Minister, after defeat in the House.  It was a very important moment. The secular parties tried to form the Government but they failed to form the Government. After that, it took 46 months from April 1999 to February 2002 to bring this resolution. After bringing that resolution, the formation of Third Front had gone haywire. This Government was formed because of that resolution. Every now and then some turbulence is coming for the UPA Government. But I do not want this holy alliance to be disturbed forever. Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru tried to bring this alliance. As long as Sardar Patel was the Home Minister, there was a ban on the communists. After his death, the ban was lifted by Pandit Nehru. He was always having a sympathy for the communists. Indira Gandhi also tried to have an alliance. She was partially successful in 1971. She was able to have an alliance with the CPI. Rajiv Gandhi also tried to have an alliance. It was too late. In 1990, after going out of the 7 Race Course Road, he invited two important Left Leaders to 10 Janpath. He was sitting on the dinning table and Shrimati Sonia Gandhi was also sitting there. At that time, he said a very important thing to the Left Leaders. He said that he was misled by the people when he was in the Government. He wanted to have an alliance with the Left and that he wanted to have an understanding with them. He was not able to do it, but only Sonia Gandhi Ji is able to do it. 

For the benefit of the House, I would like to say what happened in 1930. When Pandit Nehru was the Congress President in 1930, he went to Jalandhar. A very big meeting was organised there on a four acre plot. The maize crop was cut for this meeting. The District Congress Committee leaders organised this meeting. While he was addressing the meeting, there was a big clash between the workers. Pandit Nehru stopped his speech and asked the local leaders as to why they are fighting with each other. The local Congress leaders said that the communists have come to their meeting with the red flags. Acharya Kriplani had sent a circular saying not to allow red flags to come to the Congress meeting. That is why, our Congress workers are fighting with the Communist workers. Immediately, he asked what if the Communists come with the red flags come to our meeting. He said that the communists will bring poor people with the red flags. He also said that we must always encourage them and that we must allow them to come to our meetings. He also said that he did not want the Congress to become a party of Tatas and Birlas. He wanted the Congress Party to become a party of the poor people. That is what he said in his speech. I wanted to say this today because the Congress Party and the Left have come together to form this alliance. Every now and then some problem is coming up. I do not want this alliance to be disturbed. Many people may think that this Government has been just formed. It is not just formed. After 1999 when Shri Atal Bihari Vajpayee became the Prime Minister, a lot of hard work was put in and a lot of persuasion took place. It took 46 months to come out with a resolution in Hyderabad. Therefore, this Government should not be disturbed[r70] .

Sir, I would here like to mention about the attitude of certain people towards the poor people and the communists. I would like to quote an instance when Dr. Rajendra Prasad was the Congress President in 1939. Once Dr. Rajendra Prasad accompanied by Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru went to a village near Punjab inhabited by people belonging to Scheduled Castes. The people there offered a glass of warm milk to each of them. Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru drank that milk immediately. I have great respect for Dr. Rajendra Prasad but on that occasion he said that he was on fast on that day and therefore, he would not drink the milk. The very next day again both of them visited another village and went to a basti inhabited by people belonging to Scheduled Castes. There also, the people of the locality offered a glass of milk to both of them. They were poor people and in those days of 1939, they offered them milk. When milk was offered, Pandit Nehru drank that glass of milk immediately, but Dr. Rajendra Prasad said that he could not take the milk since he was having a stomach-ache. After having come back to the guest house, they were served beautiful lunch and Dr. Rajendra Prasad took lunch in the guest house. Someone informed Pandit Nehru that Dr. Rajendra Prasad, who did not drink the milk in the basti on reasons of stomach-ache, was then taking lunch in the guest house… (Interruptions) Pandit Nehru laughed and said: `I understand Rajen Babu’s problem.’ I only wanted to say about the attitude of some of the leaders with regard to poor people and the ones who believed and followed communism. So, these people would have to be kept in mind. The holy alliance of the Left and the Congress should not be allowed to be disturbed at all. By all means, this alliance should be saved. I would say, this is a holy alliance… (Interruptions)

Sir, I also wanted to say something about the late Rajiv Gandhi… (Interruptions) Actually I was coming to the issue of disinvestment. There has been a lot of hue and cry about 10 per cent disinvestment of shares of BHEL. Sometimes, both inside the House and outside, I request the comrades to be a little more liberal in their approach and give the Government a little bit of more freedom to function. I can understand their problem. 

Sir, coming to the provisions of the present Bill I would like to request the hon. Minister who piloted the Bill to consider increasing the number of days of employment from the proposed 100 days now to 150 days. Also, the Government should consider widening the scope of this Bill from the proposed 200 districts to 300 districts and raising the amount to be paid for employment from the proposed Rs. 60 to Rs. 70… (Interruptions)

MR. CHAIRMAN : If you continue like this, then your speech will not be recorded any more. 

DR. CHINTA MOHAN : One may ask me as to wherefrom the money would come. I am not an economist to suggest the ways. But I would like to say that the previous Government made an allocation of Rs. 2,00,000 crore for the Golden Quadrilateral project. The Government is also collecting cess on petrol and diesel. Diesel, after all, is a poor man’s oil. The Government is collecting a cess of 50 paise on diesel. I would suggest that Government should utilise this cess earned from diesel to fund this project. It would help in spreading the benefits of this project from the proposed 200 districts to 300 districts and also would help in raising the amount to be paid for employment from Rs. 60 to Rs. 70. I would request the Government to put in efforts to see that the reach of this scheme increases and it is passed. 

With these words, I conclude. 

DR. C. KRISHNAN Sir, thank you very much for giving me this opportunity to speak on this Bill. I am speaking on behalf of Marumalarchi Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam headed by my eminent and active Tamil's Leader, Thiru Vaiko of Tamil Nadu. I rise to support and welcome the National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill. This Bill aims at providing 100 days of employment in order to assure at least an assured livelihood for the poor people for 100 days in a year[snb71] . 

19.00 hrs.

Hundred days in a year may not be sufficient for the rural people. I do not know what sort of work or what nature of work will be given to them. In the rural areas, people know farming, pottery, minor electrical works, and shop keeping. What sort of work will be selected for each family in a district to give them 100 days of work remains to be settled. The wage that has been fixed is Rs. 60. Even though it is a small amount, some thing is better than nothing. Let them earn it. Those who have not been given employment in a family are to be given about fifty per cent of the wages as subsidy and with that they have to be in the house. 

This scheme will be of much use if small scale industries are involved in it, in the form of cottage industries in the villages. Promotion of cottage industries will be of much help because they will be earning throughout the year, not just 100 days. They should be given some sort of employment so that they earn throughout the year. The persons selected from the family should know the nature of job with which they will be entrusted. Some sort of training is very much needed so that people earn not only for 100 days but also for another 265 days and further more in the coming years also.

By introducing this National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, the United Progressive Government, the UPA Government, has crossed one more milestone. I should congratulate Dr. Raghuvansh Prasad Singh for formulating the Bill and to be the Minister when the Bill is introduced. 

I want the Government to take note of certain points. First, 200 districts are to be selected from the country and remaining districts are to be selected in a phased manner. That should be completed during the tenure of 14th Lok Sabha itself, not beyond that so that the programme is completed in a fast manner; people get more opportunities to work for at least 100 days in a year, and each family is guaranteed a small income. 

It is said that ten per cent of the amount to be given to the employees is to be borne by the State Governments. But eventually the State Governments are going to ask the Central Government to fund for this ten per cent also. Why not the Central Government think in terms of bearing the full 100 per cent of the wages? The compensation for the non-employed persons shall be Rs. 50. It should reach the poor persons in all cases. That has to be guaranteed. 

Then, similar job guarantee should be given for the agricultural workers and the agricultural coolies. With that the income of the rural people will be enhanced and they will get a small benefit at least. Involving small scale industries or cottage industries will be the best and the ideal way to give rural employment. Otherwise, it is going to be a waste. It is because they have to select a job which the person knows. The number of such jobs are minimum. We have to give training in small scale industry or cottage industry so that they earn throughout the year and it will be of use for the family as such.

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF DEFENCE AND MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PARLIAMENTARY AFFAIRS (SHRI BIJOY HANDIQUE): Sir, with your kind permission, I would like to inform the House that dinner will be served from 8.30 p.m. onwards for the hon. Members, members of the Press and the members of the Staff. 

SHRI NIKHILANANDA SAR Mr. Chairman, Sir, I stand in support of the Bill. Though many hon. Members are hesitant to accept it as a historical one, yet I am sure they are ready to accept it as a radical piece of legislation. At least it must be admitted as per their versions.

In this Bill, there is no provision of any permanent employment for the poor rural people nor is it for the whole country as the towns and municipalities are outside the purview of this Bill. We should first realise that it is the beginning of a new era. That much should be realised[R73] .

What is the condition of the villages? Two out of three Indians live in villages. The condition of most of the villages is beyond description. Poverty and unemployment are rampant. There is a food scarcity. There is no education, no civic amenities, lack of irrigation is there, rural indebtedness is on the increase. That is the real picture of the Indian villages. On the other hand, the poor people of the villages do not get even two square meals a day. In many parts of the country, people take leaves and roots due to hunger. Hundreds of suicides are taking place in villages. At the same time, poor mothers are selling their kids just for Rs. 10 to Rs. 15 for being unable to feed their kids. This is the grim reality. It has come to our focus through Electronic Media or Press Media. Our friends from the Opposition Benches are criticising the things but they still have not made alternative suggestions that what we should do. Now, the position is that they are not able to do any good thing in their own States. Mr. Swain made a very bad remark regarding State of West Bengal. He has already admitted in his speech that more than 50 per cent people in Orissa are below the poverty line and he is after West Bengal where BPL level is within 20 to 24 per cent and that is the position. Still, he is after West Bengal. He should know that Mr. Rajiv Gandhi, after being the Prime Minister, wanted to know in actual what should be the Panchayat. He had held a two day long meeting in Calcutta with the heads of the Panchayat bodies. Finally, he came to a conclusion that Constitution should be amended and 73rd and 74th Amendment took place afterwards. He got the experience from West Bengal. Now, he is after West Bengal. He said that Telangana is better than Orissa. What logic has he made? It is difficult to understand that. This is the position… (Interruptions)

SHRI REWATI RAMAN SINGH (ALLAHABAD): He is not listening to you. 

SHRI NIKHILANANDA SAR : However, we should know that this is a very long standing problem which we should overcome.

SHRI ANNASAHEB M.K. PATIL : May I clarify you? 

MR. CHAIRMAN : No clarifications please. You need not answer that. If you begin to answer, you will lose your time. 

SHRI NIKHILANANDA SAR : The position here is that at least 90 million people in our country are Scheduled Tribe people. This 90 million is more than the total population of many countries. What is their position? They live either in the forests or in the outskirts of the forests[bts74] .

Their life is forest-oriented. Now, they are driven out of the forest. This is the position. What has been done for them? We should think in that way. So many schemes have been started. The Assurance Scheme was there. Now, there is an Employment Guarantee Bill. One should remind that the problems will not be overcome through this Scheme only. It should be our precept that something is better than nothing. We should take it. We should start in such a way that other things can take place simultaneously.

The other thing is the land development. If you want to improve the conditions of the villagers, the land productivity should be increased. Who will be the owner of excess production? It is the kulaks of the villages and the land sharks. Therefore, the purpose will be foiled? Are they ready to take land reform measures? In West Bengal, it is a prior condition of success in Panchayats in rural areas. It must be done; otherwise, the rural development cannot take place, and it will remain in imagination only. For that reason, the land reform measures should be given priority. 

Shri Kalyan Singh calculated for 100 days. He said that only Rs. 6000 per year, that is, Rs. 500 per month. How can a person manage his family? It is a clear case of misconception. It should be realized. Now, what does a poor villager get? It is Rs. 500, which will be his additional income in a lean period. Now, what is the remuneration? It differs from State to State. There are many legal clashes. Now, this is a Central Government Scheme. But, at the same time, it will create problem from one State to another. There is no doubt that legal disputes may take place. For that reason, we thought of 75 per cent of the total national average wage. It will be something around Rs. 50. The Government has come out with a suggestion giving Rs. 60. It is not bad. At the same time, I would like to caution the Government that what are you going to do if you are not serious. The Government must be serious otherwise the people all over India will censure you whenever they get the opportunity. You have to be very serious in tackling the question of poverty.

With these words, I support the Bill.

SHRI BIR SINGH MAHATO Mr. Chairman, Sir, I rise to support this Bill. This Bill is a unique Bill and a historic Bill. This Bill is for the rural people and poor people. This Bill will have a far-reaching consequence for the people in the rural areas. The people in the rural areas are waiting for a long time for this Bill. The entire rural community has appreciated this Bill and it is also appreciated and praised by the United Nations Organisation. 

After the passing of this Bill, I hope that there will be no starvation and people will not go to towns in search of work. Also the people in the rural areas will be able to fight poverty and unemployment.

The Food for Work programme is going on in 150 districts. After the passing of this Bill, another 50 districts will be added because of the beginning of these novel schemes. 

I would like to mention some of the significant features of this Bill. There will be social audit and public scrutiny. The muster rolls, the sanction orders and all these things will be shown to the Gram Sabhas. There is no secret, and everything, budget and other works will be made available to the public. 

Sir, we are demanding right to work for a long time and this has been mentioned in our Constitution. This Bill, to some extent, gives recognition to that demand. 

Sir, amendment relating to wage rate has been brought and it says that the minimum wage rate will be not less than Rs. 60. It is all right in the States where the minimum wage rate is less than Rs. 60. But there are States where the minimum wage rate is more than Rs. 60. So, what will be the minimum wage rate in those States? I urge upon the Minister to come forward with an amendment so that the minimum wage rate of that particular State where it is more than Rs. 60 can be given to the workers.

This migration has to stop. There has to be some amount of effort made to provide employment to the rural folk so that they are not tempted to go to the urban areas. I speak specially of our State of Bihar from where there has been a regular exodus to urban cities, metropolitan cities, and other States. This Bill is an attempt to provide legal guarantee for employment to the rural folk in the countryside for at least 100 days at a minimum wage of Rs. 60 per day per head. There is a little confusion here as to what should be the minimum wage. If we peruse the Financial Memorandum attached to the Bill along with the Amendments for which a notice has been given by hon. Minister for Rural Development, it becomes clear that the minimum wages enshrined in the Act of any State or, in fact, all over the country, vary from Rs. 25 to Rs. 135. It is at an average of Rs. 60 that the Financial Memorandum has calculated the overall financial implication at about Rs. 20,000 crore. It is with this in mind that the matter has been clarified. 

I read from the notice of amendments given by hon. Minister for Rural Development regarding wage rate relating to Section 6 which says: 

“Notwithstanding anything contained in the Minimum Wage Act, 1948, the wage rate for the purpose of Clause (a) of sub-section (1) of Section 22 shall be Rs. 60.….”

Then it further goes on to say :

“…provided that the Central Government may by notification specify the wage rate at a rate not less than Rs. 60 from time to time.”

It is, therefore, quite clear that the wage rate in a State if it happens to be in excess of Rs. 60, will be the wage rate for that State. And if the wage rate happens to be less than Rs. 60 in any State, the wage rate there will be a minimum of Rs. 60. So, there should be no apprehension about, as our friend Shri Dharmendra Pradhan had, that there is some kind of a fraud being played through this Act; the wage that is being paid to the labour is less than Rs.60. Nothing of that kind is going to happen. The minimum wage will be Rs. 60, and if it happens to be more than Rs. 60 in any State, as per the Wage Act applicable to that State, it will be that wage which will be applicable. 

Sir, there is also a provision in this that where the authorities concerned fail to provide employment to an applicant, there is a provision for paying that applicant a penalty, the kind of a dole. I commend the UPA Government for bringing in the concept of social security here, which so far had been lacking. There have been a number of schemes that have been implemented in the country in the past 15 years. But the concept of social security was lacking there. If this is implemented, it will be a very welcome move, and I support it.

There is, of course, a great fear of corrupt practices being implied in the implementation of this Scheme. This can be done at any level. The proposed Act has a provision, which gives us confidence that the Government is determined to see that corruption is not allowed[t81] . 

I may be permitted to read that provision, which says:

“The application from any person wanting employment could be made at three levels. It could be made at the level of the panchayat, at the level of the block, and at the level of the district.”

There is, therefore, some kind of a cross-referencing which would ensure that there are no fake applications or there is no attempt by the authorities concerned to keep an application pending for more than the required time. After the required time stipulated in the Act as 15 days is over, it would be a question of passing a dole, which would not be justified. It is in these cases that some corrective action would have to be taken. If it is found that some fraud has been played by authorities concerned, they would have to face criminal action. If it were found that there has been genuine laxity, there would be a fine.

I would appeal to the hon. Minister that if there were to be a criminal prosecution, it would take time and knowing the criminal justice system that obtains in our country, it would not be wise to allow the people concerned to launch a criminal prosecution. Why could we not examine imposing a greater fine? For instance, instead of Rs. 500, which has been prescribed for those who are found guilty of laxity, it could be to Rs. 1,000. For those who are found to have played a kind of fraud, it could be raised to Rs. 10,000. If these amounts were increased, it would be possible to provide a very great deterrent to people who want to indulge in corrupt practices. In fact, the increase in the amount of fine is something which has also been prescribed and recommended by the 154th Report of the Law Commission. So, this principle could be made applicable here also.

Two hundred districts, which are economically backward, have been proposed to be covered by this scheme. It is expected that these 200 districts would enjoy the benefits of this Scheme in the next two or three years. If indeed this Scheme is implemented honestly, it should be possible to reap the benefits of this Scheme in at least two years. So, why is it not possible to extend the benefits of this Scheme to all the districts in India, which would be about 550 to 600, within a period of five years? This is something which I wish to submit before the hon. Minister. He might consider extending this Scheme to all the districts in India within a period of five years.

Unfortunately, my district and constituency, Aurangabad, in Bihar is one of the 170 economically backward districts but it has not been included in the Food-for-work Programme. I appeal to the hon. Minister that this time around, when this Scheme is implemented, Aurangabad should be included in it so that it could give us a great deal of relief.

I had referred to the question of dole earlier. It is not a very happy thing to have a dole of some kind but if at all a dole is being given it is not the intention and any case should be for a basic minimum period. That should be our intention. That is why I suggested that instead of 200 districts being covered in the next two or three years, attempts should be made to cover the entire lot of districts in the country in a period of five years. If that is done, automatically, it would be possible for us to increase the number of people who get employment in the rural sector. The previous Government had announced that it would come up with one crore jobs throughout the period but at least this would provide a big fillip to people who are in our rural countryside and the concept of dole would go. It would be a genuine attempt at providing employment to rural people in the countryside.

SHRI UDAY SINGH : Sir, I will try and finish it in less time than that. This Bill at least has the potential of becoming a historic Bill. It is being called a historic Bill today. Sir, I am in complete agreement with the need for this Bill, but in equal disagreement with the manner in which it is sought to be implemented. 

The Congress Government has governed this country for longer than most parties. But it is not learning from its experience. It is not bracing to face the challenges posed by a wretchedly faulty public delivery system. Therefore, it is lending itself open to being charged with repeated wrong-doings at great public expense which is an extremely serious matter. It is said that the only thing more painful thing than learning from experience is not learning from experience.

If he has not, then he is wronged, and if he has, then this Government has certainly again displayed the ostrich syndrome. 

Sir, if I may ask what should our holistic approach of our responsibilities, towards our poor actually be. We must strive to give them a livable house, safe drinking water, primary health and educational facilities and, above all, an opportunity to make a decent living for self and family. But is it not time that the Government really asks itself as to how many different schemes do we actually require to fulfil there very basic needs? At present, I think, there are more than two dozen such schemes which are running and the reason given for running so many schemes is that each scheme needs a close monitoring to reach the target audience or to reach the target group. But who, may I ask, are we charging with the responsibility to reach this to the target group? This is going back to the same District Magistrate, to the same DRDA official in States. So, while the Government says or pretend that one comprehensive Bill will become too unwieldy, it is assuming that these district officials possess some super-natural powers and they will do justice to all the schemes that they are presiding over. I am sorry to say that this Bill will be one more addition to that long list which is already there in the districts.

SHRI RUPCHAND PAL (HOOGHLY): Thank you, Sir. I will be very brief or should I say as brief as possible. The Left Parties expected that this Government would move ahead on the right track and fulfil, as early as possible, the assurances made to the people of this country when the Left Parties decided to support the new UPA Government from outside on the basis of the NCMP. Now, we are happy that, at least, one assurance with regard to employment guarantee for the rural people is shortly to be implemented by this Government. But it is only a beginning, and we have miles to go. I am saying this because only 200 districts are being covered, and the rural poor are still to be addressed. Therefore, the hon. Minister while replying to the debate must assure this House that not only within a period of 5 years, but, as early as possible, the case of the rest of millions of our mute, hungry people is also going to be addressed.

In India, there are two Indias. One India is glamorous, billionaire, and a handful spending lots of money in five-star culture. On the other hand, there is an India of 85 per cent or 90 per cent of the population living in hunger, destitution, and who are downtrodden and underprivileged. There have been several schemes to provide them employment and to provide them food, but most of them have gone astray as there have been targets that have been missed. Although, no constitutional guarantee can be given, but legal guarantee is being given here. I think, it would become an irreversible programme irrespective of the complexion of the Government, and whoever might be in the Government would have to pursue it. Therefore, it is historic in this sense. There have been programmes like garibi hatao, 20-Point programme, etc., but there have not been any guarantees for it. Now, for the first time it is being done.

There are people who have been raising different issues. Where would the funds come for it? I would say that there is no dearth of funds. In a country where out of 1.1 billion people only 80,000 people are declaring that their income is Rs. 10 lakh, while at the same time luxury cars costing more than Rs. 15 lakh are being sold. Therefore, there is large-scale evasion, black money, etc. If the Government is serious, then it can even take into the account the recommendations made by its own Committees for collection of tax arrears to plug the loopholes for tax evasion, and there would be no dearth of money. 

There have been some other issues like minimum wages. A question has been raised that all other schemes like poverty alleviation scheme, etc. -- now currently in vogue -- may be merged. What will happen by doing it? Is the minimum wage that is already being given in other areas -- barring this area -- also going to be reduced or not? This was a question raised by no less a person than the former Prime Minister of this country Shri V. P. Singh. Therefore, it must be addressed. But the House should be assured that this is the beginning, and there are miles to go. 

It is also very amusing that the NDA and the BJP are trying to ask : “why is it not being done? Why the urban poor is not being addressed in it? Why only 200 districts are being covered in it?” At the time of severe drought we have been repeatedly asking the same people to introduce the Food-for-Work programme. But it all fell on deaf ears[ak85] .

They did not care for that. Now, we are happy that at least this Government is taking care of them. Although we have serious differences with them, we want to convince them that the Left is not against reforms. The question is, reforms in whose interest or reforms in what direction. Millions of our people are hungry. If the reforms mean that their hunger should be addressed, then I say that you are on the right track of reforms. 

Sir, I do not want to take much time. I support this Bill. The merger of the schemes may create certain problems. The quality of the schemes should be such that they create durable assets, like water resources, irrigation, which may increase productivity; it may be part of the ‘Bharat Nirman’ process; it may add to the purchasing capacity and contribute to the acceleration of the industrial process. 

The empowerment issue has emphasised that womenfolk should be given priority as it will stop migration because when the men go out or migrate, all the work is done by the womenfolk. Rightly, the Panchayati Raj system should be involved; the Gram Sabhas should be involved. It is a historic step. We should be cautious, we should be careful, we should be serious about the implementation and extending it to the rest of the districts and to the urban areas. 

Due to the time constraint, I wish to conclude my speech. I support this Bill and I believe that the Minister while replying to the debate will give the full assurance to the nation that they are serious about the achieving the goal within a short while. 

SHRI AJAY MAKEN (NEW DELHI): Sir, with your permission, I beg to lay the text of my speech on the Table of the House.

MR. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Yes, you can do so. Is there anybody else who wants to lay his or her speech on the Table of the House?

SHRI AJAY MAKEN Chairman Sir, I thank you for the opportunity to speak on National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, 2005. I consider myself to be extremely fortunate to speak in support of this Bill and thus in turn be a part of the History. This Bill will prove to be a milestone in the Indian history. Thus, it can be well imagined, why the opposition is getting jittery on this bill. Everyone knows that the people on account of their dismal performance at rural development and employment generation front rejected the NDA government. Their tenure is marked by jobless growth. Only the share markets went up and the rural folk continued to commit suicide.

However, I observed a very remarkable behavior amongst the BJP members today. But before going on to it, I shall refer to some of the statements made by their leaders in and outside the Parliament. They first complained about just 150 districts being covered in the programme. But we have not only increased it to 200, but also an undertaking that the programme will be implemented in the rest of the country within 5 yrs. This made NDA jittery. They started asking for universal application. We agreed and said that instead of BPL households, it would be universally applicable to all households. Then instead of being satisfied, they have now started saying that they want it to be universally applicable on all persons instead of households. It is strange that initially, one of the former BJP President, in a statement alleged that the Government is handing over the bill to a specially formed select committee and not to the standing committee on rural development (which is chaired by Sh. Kalyan Singh, a BJP leader). This allegation was also totally unfounded when the bill was handed over to the standing committee only. Then many suggestions made by the committee, such as social audit by the gram sabha etc, were also incorporated in the Bill. So the BJP is totally dumbfounded 

* Speech was laid on the Table.

and speechless now. So today they have devised a strategy. Instead of fully criticizing the Bill, they have now decided to not criticize the Bill, but to some how try and dilute the credit, which is going to the Congress party, and Smt. Sonia Gandhi. But let me assure them that the country knows it very well, as to who is behind the bill and how this bill is an extension of Maharshtra State Employment Guarantee Act, which was introduced and practiced by the Congress party in the State.

It has been argued by some members of the BJP and NDA, that the Bill should also be extended to the urban areas. They are perhaps oblivious to the demands of the urban areas. They perhaps do not know that such type of schemes would be a failure in the urban areas. I would just like to tell the house that an NGO, Aashray Adhikar Abhiyan AAA, in the year 2000 conducted a survey of homeless persons of Delhi. They found out that, 89% of the homeless and shelterless people are employed in the unorganized sector. Propagationists of such schemes in the urban areas perhaps do not know that any person who offers his services for daily wages in a Chowk of the city, gets work every two days out of three days. Thus the problem in urban areas is not that of employment but that of underemployment. The problem is of shelter more than any thing else.

I would like to present before this august house, very stratling figures. If we look at the ten year figures of population growth and compare it with that of GDP growth, we will see that when the GDP has grown more in the average of a ten year span, then the population in urban areas has decreased for that particular period.

But the question arises, as to why is there a need for this bill? Because in 1980s, average GDP grew by 5.2% and employment growth by 2.7%. Surprisingly when in thw 1990s, the GDP grew by 6.7 % ( 1.5% more than the previous decade), the employment growth slowed down to 1.07% from 2.7%.

10th Plan document also says that by the end of 10th plan, there would be a backlog of 35 million unemployed. In the eighth plan, the amount of money spend on rural development was 13%, but it slid down to 5% now. Sampoorn Gramin Rojgar Yojna (SGRY) was able to generate only at an average 20 man days of employment in BPL households annually for the year 2002-03 and 2003-04.

Thus there was a crying need for such a scheme and I am thankful to UPA chairperson, Smt Sonia Gandhi and our Prime Minister Dr Manmohan Singh to have brought such a Bill.

Besides experience of Maharashrta also shows that this bill, when enacted would meet considerable success. In maharashtra:-

- This bill is successfully working since last 30 yrs

- It has resulted in geration of 370 crore mandays

- Rs 9000 crores have already been spent through this scheme

- In the 1990s decade, 10 lakh hectare has been made fit for horticulture

- Agriculture labour now get better wages

- In many areas, it has been reported that 40 to 50% of women get the work

Amongst numerous advantages of the Bill, I would like to mention the following:-

- For the first time a poor village-folk will now get a right in the form of guarantee of a Parliamentary Act, to ask for something from the Governemnt.

- Through this Act, the size of the development programme shall be determined by the workers and not by the officials

- Panchayats, shall be the nodal agency for planning. Thus planning for spending 40,000 crores would be decided at the lowest level.The planning process would be from bottom to top and not from top to bottom.

- The guarantee word shall increase the flexibility of this bill. Thus in times of need more work and otherwise less.

- This will stop migration of workers from rural areas.

- This Bill if enacted, shall not only generate employment, but also develop the rural areas.

- In this Bill, a number of new kind of works have also been added, which can be undertaken. These works will improve the agriculture production and also condition of agriculture land. It will favourably tilt ecological balance.

- I would like to mention here an experience of Madhya Pradesh. The Digvijay Singh government through land reforms, gave agriculture land to landless SC/ST people. But the productive land were at many places, not handed over to the deserving SC/ST; and only those plots of land not fit for agriculture were only allowed to be taken over by the SC/ST. Now the Bill provides for the irrigation works to be undertaken in the land of SC/ST. This Bill thus would help in land reforms also.

At this juncture, I have some suggestions to make :-

-We should use the Right to Information to oversee the success of this Bill. NGOs should be encouraged to come in and act as watchdogs. But I would also call upon the Political Parties to train their cadre and take the place of NGOs where there are none. I would also congratulate our leader Smt. Sonia Gandhi who has already entrusted upon this task to Seva Dal of Congress party.

- We should have a solid financial foundation. This could be achieved only through improved Tax-GDP ratio. In 1987-88 the tax –GDP ratio was 10.6%, now it is 9.3%. If are able to achieve the Tax-GDP ratio of pre-reforms period, we may generate more than 35,000 crores. This amount can take care of this scheme

- There should be proper selection of districts. I would suggest that the names of districts should not be fixed. But after annual review on various important parameters, depending upon various natural factors, new districts should be allowed to replace some old ones.

- Skill training and better planning and sequencing of work should be taken care of.

In the end, I will quote Gandhi Ji :-

“ The Blood of the villages is the cement with which the edifices of the cities is built. I want the blood, that is today inflating the arteries of the cities, to run once again in the blood vessels of the villages”

SHRI M. APPADURAI Hon. Deputy Speaker Sir, I thank the Chair for giving me this opportunity to speak on the National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill. I welcome this move by the Government to reach the rural poor directly after 58 years of independence during the tenure of 14th Lok Sabha. I welcome and extend support to this Bill on behalf of our party Communist Party of India. I am happy that this Bill is a consummation of the efforts put in by the left parties in this House.

The Bill seeks to extend this scheme to 200 districts and I would like to point out that this is not adequate and other districts with rural areas must also get a similar scheme. It is a welcome step that Departments concerned will be responsible for implementing various schemes. Another welcome feature of the Bill pertains to the non-inclusion of contract system. I also want to urge upon the Government to ensure proper monitoring to keep away mechanisation and use of machines in schemes to be carried out under this Act. Only 4 districts out of 29 districts in Tamil Nadu have been covered in the ambit of this Act. 

I would like to draw your attention to the fact that southern districts in Tamil Nadu have been neglected. Tirunelveli, Tuticorin, Ramanathapuram, Sivaganga and Virudhunagar districts that come under my Thenkasi constituency are drought prone districts and worst hit by caste and communal riots hitting hard the deprived classes in the rural areas. Hence I urge upon the Union Government to include these districts also in the ambit of this Act to benefit especially the downtrodden people of these districts.

In order to accomplish the purpose for which the legislation is made, proper vigil and monitoring mechanism must be in place. This Act lists out the works that are to be carried out in the rural areas. I would like to emphasise that small irrigation projects, building of small tanks and reservoirs, laying of village roads, __________________________________________________________________*Translation of the speech originally delivered in Tamil.

sanitation and drinking water schemes and housing must get priority in the implementation of this Act.

It is a boon to the rural poor that they get a guaranteed job opportunity directly in developing infrastructure facilities in their local areas. We must also bear in mind that this enactment in itself is not enough to alleviate poverty in the country. The minimum wage fixed is Rs 60 as per this Act. It may be revised as early as you can. Wherever deviations are noticed such jobs must be taken away from the ambit of this scheme and such works must be stopped.

In order to take the entire benefit to the rural poor, Centre must enact Land Reforms Act. “Land to the tiller not to the farmer” is what we want to reiterate when we talk of land reforms. Our former Prime Minister Pandit Jawaharlal Nehru said that State Governments must endeavour to bring about land reforms in their respective States. Distributing lands is different from land reforms. To implement this Act and to cover 200 districts, 63000 crores of rupees would be required. If it is to be extended further 1 lakh 40 thousand crores of rupees would be needed. I would like to impress upon the Union Government that this viable Act must be reenacted to cover urban poor also.

One adult from every household would be eligible to get the guaranteed job. If the household has a joint family then the head count may not be practical giving rise to practical problems. Wiping out poverty in its entirity may not be possible. This Act is but a noble effort. Rural women the poorest of the poor will get priority while the beneficiaries are identified. It has been ensured 33% reservation would be earmarked for them. Considering the fact that 34% of our people are much below in the social strata and far below poverty line, we must increase the minimum wage and the number of days of work. Rs 6000 per annum is not sufficient and calls for an upward revision. 

The Central contribution of 90% and States’ contribution of 10% are there for this programme but it needs to be ensured that there are no stoppages due to non-availability of earmarked funds. Proper care, constant vigil, able monitoring can ensure the successful implementation of this programme. 

Let me conclude my speech welcoming this Bill.

SHRIMATI TEJASWINI SEERAMESH I thank you hon. Deputy Speaker, Sir, for giving me this opportunity. I rise to support this National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill brought forward by this UPA Government in this august House.

MR. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: You can speak only for four or five minutes.

SHRIMATI TEJASWINI SEERAMESH : Sir, I feel very proud in congratulating my UPA Government, UPA Chairperson, our hon. Prime Minister and, of course, the champion of the poorest of the poor, our Rural Development Minister Dr. Raghuvansh Prasad Singhji. I would also like to thank our Chairman, Standing Committee on Rural Development, Shri Kalyan Singhji, who, under his leadership, ensured consensus on these recommendations. No doubt, it is a historic Bill. Though my friends in the Opposition will not agree with me, it is a historic and revolutionary Bill. But I am having my own arguments. 

Sir, this Bill, which ensures job to the unemployed youths in the largest democracy, that is, India, is the first of its kind in the world. Our Government is candid and honest in accepting that unemployment in the rural sector is a challenging national problem. It is honestly trying to address this problem by bringing a ray of hope among these hopeless millions of unemployed youths in the rural sector, who are suffering from illiteracy, ill-health and other infrastructure problems. Sir, in my view, unemployment is an undeclared death sentence passed on to the millions of youths whereas this country requires their dynamic energy for nation building. It is not only a social crime, but a national crime also. We cannot reject our younger brothers and sisters from participating in nation building. That is why I see a direct link between unemployment and terrorism, naxalism and dowry deaths. I also see a direct link between unemployment and prostitution where our beloved sisters, mothers and daughters are selling their bodies to feed their children and families. It is a social crime. We should, rising above party differences, address this. I hope my brothers on the other side will accept this. 

Sir, a hungry mouth or stomach will not understand what is dignity, what is humanity or patriotism. Even though they are patriotic youths, but this nation rejected them. Whether we belong to this side or that side, we must admit that as a nation, we failed to address this unemployment problem. But, at least, this UPA Government has accepted this and admitted that it is a problem; let us honestly try to address this problem in a challenging manner. 

Sir, in this Bill, there is one thing which I would like to appreciate. My brother from the Opposition, Shri Swain, has expressed some doubts and said that things like afforestation, watershed, linking of villages, and all that are unproductive. I would like to bring it to the notice of this House that in the rural sector, the women, youths or these boys are not skilled labourers. You do not look at things in a direct manner. Even irrigation can generate lots of job opportunities in agriculture sector. When they get some perks through these activities, it will generate a lot of opportunities in the education sector. It will bring some confidence and that is very important. It will bring some hope and will really bring some patriotism. My country will be steering like that. 

I, now, come to my last point. I would like to mention here that Indiraji dreamt to empower the women. We cannot empower women through speeches alone. We must ensure one-third reservation for them in the jobs under this scheme. Then only we can have this empowerment of women where a mother will not face a situation wherein she sells her dear babies. That is why, I would say that this Bill is not everything. This Bill is not going to bring heavens to this nation. We are not in such illusions. It is definitely an honest and a bold attempt to address this problem. I would request that the whole House must stand united to address this problem.

With these words, I support this Bill. 

MR. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Now, Shri Sita Ram Singh. You may please take only four minutes.

SHRI L. RAJAGOPAL Mr. Deputy-Speaker, Sir, I rise to support this National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill. At the very outset I would like to recollect the words of Mahatmaji, who said: `The cost of liberty becomes a mockery if the prices to be paid is wholesale destruction of those who are to enjoy this liberty.’ 

Sir, today we are witnessing huge unemployment both in rural as well as in urban areas. People need employment so that they can live with dignity, they can live with confidence, they can have a source of income and also they can feed their families and live happily. But unfortunately we have the liberty to speak and express ourselves in this august House in as many words as we want, but in reality what is happening in terms of deeds is that words are not getting translated into deeds. That is the reason why this Government, headed by Dr. Manmohan Singh and with the blessings of Shrimati Sonia Gandhi and support of the alliance partners, has brought forward this historic Bill, namely, the National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill[snb95] . 

A lot of people think what is historic or unique about this Bill. Nowhere in the world we have the National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill. This Bill ensures that every member of a family gets work for minimum 100 days. That is the reason this Bill is called historic and unique one. Creation of work is not a new thing. It may be unique in this modern world. But if you go back, 5,000 years, when there were floods or when there was lack of work, the rulers of Egypt created work, by building pyramids. In those days pyramids might have been unproductive assets. But looking back, in today's world, the same pyramids are creating a lot of income to the country by way of tourism. Similarly, in India, we have Taj Mahal. All of us know that Taj Mahal is the symbol of India. In those days it took 20 years to build that and thousands of people were involved in its construction. Creation of work has been there. Today, the same Taj Mahal stands as a symbol of India and a lot of tourism is generated because of such monuments. That is the reason this Government chose to come out with this Act so that we can create useful assets. It could be restoration of water bodies, it could be water harvesting; it could be afforestation; or it could be linking of roads. We can do these things in order to create work for rural poor so that youth, women and other segments of the population get employment. We need to understand the importance of this. It is not that we are giving them Rs. 60 per day. A lot of people say that we are giving them only Rs. 500 per month. It is a misconception. It is not that they are earning only Rs. 500. But we are giving them a source of guarantee so that everybody works with dignity. It is not that they work for only 100 days. Once work is created, the work could be carried on for the whole of the year and work can be created for hundreds of hours which can be given to the rural poor. People ask as to why we cannot extend this universally, that is to the urban areas also. We need to understand that we need to start somewhere. Once you arrest the migration of rural poor to urban areas that can be achieved. That can be achieved only by addressing the issue of unemployment in rural areas. Once employment is created in rural areas and the flight of rural poor to urban areas is arrested, there will not be any unemployment problem in urban areas. That is the reason this Government has started and initiated this Act, covering 200 districts, to start with, in rural areas. 

We also need to understand that at what stage this Government came in. This Government came in at a stage when there was a lot of communal hatred, when there was a lot of bloodshed, when the whole country was divided into regions and communities. This Government came at that stage. The earlier Government, the NDA Government did not focus on nation building or Bharat Nirman. They were interested in destroying places of worship rather than building nations, rather than creating work. That is the reason the entire country was engulfed in darkness. At that stage, this Government came bearing a torch showing them light. At this juncture, I would like to recall what Mr. John F. Kennedy once said. He said:

“We are not here to curse the darkness, but we are here to light a candle so that we can guide the future generation to a safe and sane Future. ”

That is the reason this Government has brought in the theme of Bharat Nirman. 

At this stage I would like to tell the House what the Andhra Pradesh Government is doing in that State. There the Government is investing Rs. 46,000 crore for building projects for irrigation. Today we are witnessing good rainfall and there is flood. But at times it does not rain at all and there is drought. So, we have to ensure that the rain we have received during the best years is used during the lean periods. That is the reason we need to build reservoirs like Nagarjunasagar, Bhakra-Nangal and Hirakud. The Government of Andhra Pradesh is also building 8 lakh houses for rural poor every year. The Government of India is building 15 lakh houses and the Government of Andhra Pradesh is building 8 lakh houses per year so that a lot of employment is created and a lot of storage capacity is created by building these dams so that water can be stored and used. 

21.10 hrs. (Shri Varkala Radhakrishnan in the Chair) 

Here, I would like to cite the example of the smallest creature in the world, that is ant. See how it plans, how it keeps on working. It is the smallest creature in the world, whereas human beings are the most intelligent creature. We need to understand how ants function[r96] .

It keeps on working. You never see ants being stationary. It always carries something not only for today’s needs but for future needs. So, it keeps on storing for future needs and builds up capacity for future needs. We need to draw example from that. We need to understand all these things. … (Interruptions)

MR. CHAIRMAN : Please conclude.

SHRI L. RAJAGOPAL : Sir, I would like to say the last point. … (Interruptions)

MR. CHAIRMAN: It is night now. 

… (Interruptions)

MR. CHAIRMAN: We will have to conclude it before midnight. 

SHRI L. RAJAGOPAL : Similarly, this Act will definitely empower the people and will ensure that people live with dignity. So, it is a good beginning. Definitely, this Government will ensure that this would spread to all over India and cover both rural and urban areas.

MR. CHAIRMAN : Hon. Member, please cooperate. Now the time is 9.45 p.m. I know, you would not conclude yourself, that is why I am appealing like this. 

SHRI B. MAHTAB Respected Deputy Speaker Sir, I stand here to discuss about the Rural Employment Guarantee Bill today. At the outset I must say that people in this country have a love-hate relationship with mathematics, a favourite school subject for some, but just a bad memory for many others.

Mathematics is cold and calculative. There is no grays. It is always black and white.

Still a large number of people say mathematics is their favourite.

Raghuvansh Babu is a student of Mathematics.

I don’t know whether he is cold but all of us know he is calculative.

The Government is going to offer 100 days of employment a year to one member from ‘every’ rural household. ‘Poor’ being amended by the ‘advice’ of the Left. However, in practice, the programme would automatically screen out the non-poor, since only minimum wages are to be paid. Only the bottom 31 percent of the rural population spend less than Rs. 380 per capita per month in 2003, the average annual household expenditure for the group as a whole being Rs. 18375/-.

I hope being a Master in Mathematics the Minister can find out who is having the last laugh?

I come to my second point, now. As all of us are aware that the rural population in 2006 is estimated to be 79.83 crores. This would put the number of “poor” rural household in the country at 4.95 crores.

Providing employment at the rate of Rs. 60 per day for 100 days in a year would entail an expenditure of less than Rs. 30000 crores in the whole country.

So far so good.

For the benefit of the rural folk.

* Speech was laid on the Table.

But the question which still remains unanswered are –

(a) as the State Council shall prepare a list of preferred works for different areas, there is no specific time period mentioned to prepare the Project Report; there by making it only open ended but also leave scope for complacency.

(b) The Standing Committee had recommended that Fifth Schedule and Sixth Schedule areas in the country which are the most backward and people residing there are the poorest, should be included in the first phase.

You have added 50 more districts to the 150 most backward districts. These districts were chosen on 3 criterion - specified by the Planning Commission to take up National Food for Work Programme.

Yet, some Districts were left out. Orissa though had 18 districts included, still 10 more qualified districts are yet to be included.

Tell us, have you included the rest 10 districts of Orissa in those 200 districts or not in this first phase?

(c) Thirdly, what mechanism you want to formulate to plug loopholes, which has given rise to corruption? Is CAG competent to verify the disbursement of wages, under this Bill. If not, are you going to make provisions for this? So that stringent action can be taken against the officials, who are in charge of this scheme.

(d) Further, as durable assets are to be created by this scheme, no where did I find in the Bill that the Government is interested to find out the quality of work is to be measured. NO attempt is there to fix parameters for various schemes or works nor any central evaluation and monitoring mechanism is envisaged.

If this is the case, why would one not believe that thousands of crores of rupees will go down the drain?

Raghuvansha Babu, as Ph. D in Mathematics you are aware that there is only one right answer to a question.  But you are also a master politicians from vaishali too and you know, there is never only one right answer to one problem.

I admire you for the deft footwork you have done to bypass the Oxford and Harvard boys. Yet a lot more is necessary to be done to overcome corruption.

One should not forget that the Planning Commission has stated that the National Rural Employment Guarantee Scheme would not need more than Rs. 13 thousand crores in the first year. You have also said that Food for Work Programme would be covered from the budgetary allocation of Rs. 24 thousand crores to the rural sector. That takes care of the funding aspect. But the question before us is what efforts be made for successful implementation of the programme? Firstly, although the Bill proposes to empower the panchayats to have the final say in implementing and monitoring projects, the vested interests often forge a nexus and siphon off the money intended for development.

The Rs. 9 crore fraud detected recently in employment guarantee scheme is Maharashtra is the latest example. Second is, will the States be able to contribute their share? And lastly, will the fiscal deficit remain within acceptable limits?

It is not a cynic’s view point but questions which need to be deliberate upon and answered be given to. With political will and support the Bill will be passed, no doubt, but the question, if remain unanswered, will not augur well for the nation.

With these words, I conclude.

SHRI RAVICHANDRAN SIPPIPARAI Sir, share market index is soaring high; foreign reserves touch upon 6 lakh crores of rupees mark; annual growth rate of our economy is pegged at 7%; all these indices promise that India will be emerging in the next 25 years a great economic power. Apart from showing concern about providing the basic infrastructural need there is a need to meet the basic needs of about 30 crores of people who live below the poverty line. We now deliberate on a Bill that comes to the aid of about 20 crores of agricultural labour who live in the rural areas of the country. It is a new milestone of UPA’s governance that has a human face about it. I heartily welcome the National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill.

Contract system is being abolished and use of machines is shunned. These are but the salient features of this Bill which seeks to involve people and employ people in implementing schemes that are to be taken up under the scheme of things envisaged in this Bill. It is also provided for in this Bill to give compensation in the form of unemployment allowance for the days on which the identified workers are not provided with job. The rural poor can now get a social security somewhat similar to that of the workers of the organised sector. When 20 women are engaged in a particular work, one among them would be entrusted with full pay the job of taking care of any child under 6 years of age who might have been brought to that work spot. This is one of the appreciable aspects of this Bill. An ex gratia payment of Rs 10000 would be paid to any worker who dies while engaged to work under this scheme. Similar features make this Bill a significant Bill and a historical one.

Our Union Minister for Rural Development Dr Raghuvansh Prasad is a socialist with a humanitarian outlook and takes effort to uplift the lot of the rural poor. At this juncture I would like to bring to your notice the findings of a survey __________________________________________________________________*Translation of the speech originally delivered in Tamil.

conducted recently in 6 States by the students of Jawaharlal Nehru University about the implementation of integrated rural development projects. It has been found out that the implementation is wrought with several flaws in 5 States that were surveyed. They had found out that proper rosters were not maintained. In the light of this I would like to urge upon the Centre that let this NREG Programme be taken up with a spirit of commitment and vigilance. 

This gigantic programme that seeks to provide jobs to 4 crore people at an expense of 40,000 crores of rupees must be handled with care and vigil. Only then the objectives could be achieved. 

The doyen and darling of the Tamil masses late lamented Anna Durai said that we must endeavour to bring smile in the saddened faces of the poor to see God Himself there. I find a serious attempt at it is being made by our hon. Rural Development Minister Dr Raghuvansh Prasad Singh. He is striving to bring happiness in about 5 crore rural families and I welcome and support his move on behalf of Marumalarchi Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam and on behalf of our leader Vaiko. 

Let me conclude my speech thanking the Chair.

SHRI LALIT MOHAN SUKLABAIDYA Mr. Chairman, Sir, I stand to support the National Employment Guarantee Bill, 2004.

Unemployment has now become a common feature of our social set up, though we have a huge human resource which we cannot employ in productive purpose.

The Bill seeks to provide employment to at least one person from each family who is ready to work. This is the first realistic approach towards solution of the huge unemployment problem of the country which could increase our gross domestic product.

Our previous attempts at upliftment of the rural economy could not deliver the expected results due to the huge population growth and ineffective management. For generation of employment for the rural population, we tried many programmes but the number of people unemployed at present indicates that these programmes could not deliver the things. For this we need to promote efficiency in management and our delivery system needs to be overhauled. The system itself should be made cautious for irregularities. Otherwise, it might jeopardise the good and sincere wishes of the UPA Government to eradicate rural poverty.

For launching an assault on poverty and unemployment, the scheme of 100 days’guaranteed employment for eligible persons, one person per family, is a bold step taken by the UPA Government. In fact, it is a turning point in the Indian economy, especially in the management of unemployment and population. Implementation of this law would be a landmark achievement of the Government towards eradication of rural poverty.

The people who would be employed would have faith in themselves because of 100 days’ employment security. This would give them earning and a sense of joining in productive work. But, one household as defined in the Bill, may consist of more than one family. For the purpose of guaranteed employment this should be taken into account. 

I wish to read out here the definition of ‘household’as mentioned in the Bill, which says:

“… the member of a family related with each other by blood, by marriage or adoption, and normally residing together … ”

MR. CHAIRMAN : Hon. Member, it would be better if you lay the remaining part of your speech instead of reading it out.

SHRI LALIT MOHAN SUKLABAIDYA : Yes, Sir. I may please be permitted to lay the remaining part of my speech. 

*We became independent in 1947, with slightly more than 33 crores of people, and today our number of unemployed people equals almost that same figure. We are 17 per cent of world population but we share only 1.8 per cent of world GDP. There is no dearth of demand but purchasing power is low. So what we need – we need to generate income by producing more and more goods and services by utilizing our resources both human and natural.

Our Honourable leader, Shrimati Sonia Gandhi pointed out that the remuneration is not dole – but they have to work to earn. We have to make Bharat Nirman within four years time. But we need manpower for building special infrastructure in rural areas, namely six components namely, Irrigation, Roads, Water-supply, Housing, Rural Electrification and rural telecom connectivity.

We can very well engage our people who will get 100 days employment in the work of Bharat Nirman and other projects drawn by competent authorities including post reconstruction works of flood and other natural calamities.

Another point which I want to mention in rural areas is that there is a specific class of people in my state Assam who are working but are not getting salary for years. Many of them have retired but without any benefits.

*…*This part of speech was laid on the Table.

These people were employed in venture schools and working without remuneration. They are waiting to get remuneration when their services would be provincialised. My request is that these people should also be covered under this scheme. Even for 100 days if they can get 6000 rupees per year, this amount can also benefit them till taking over of their services. These teachers of venture educational institutions deserve to be remunerated.

I thank Hon'ble Minister Raghuvansh Ji for moving this Bill for providing social security in one hand and on the other hand improving the quality of human life by generating income and confidence among rural population. 

Lastly, I want to quote John F. Kennedy, "If a free society cannot help the many who are poor, it cannot save the few who are rich".

Thank you sir for giving me a chance to speak.

MR. DEPUTY-SPEAKER: Thank you, Mr. Ravi Prakash Verma. No, I would not be able to give you more time to speak. Thank you.

Next is Shri Varkala Radhakrishnan.

SHRI VARKALA RADHAKRISHNAN I support the Bill. This is only a beginning and not an end in itself. I do not claim it to be a historic attempt. We can make it historic, but claiming it historic is not correct. 

Now, the Bill as schemed has many inherent weaknesses. I do not take this opportunity to point out all those inherent weaknesses, but one thing I must make it clear that this Bill has to be implemented through a sincere effort through a committed bureaucracy. The present bureaucracy is quite inefficient, insufficient and unfit for implementing this people’s Bill, which is to benefit crores of people who are in the rural areas, in the villages. 

Now, we have our own experience. We have passed the Right to Information Bill in the previous Session, which is very much connected with this Bill. So far, it was not notified. So far, the rules have not been framed. It may take some more months to do that. Now, bottlenecks have been created in framing the rules. There is a dispute as to whether the correspondence between the Executive and the Rashtrapathi Bhawan should be brought under the purview of Right to Information Act. So, it will take months for the bureaucracy to notify the rules as well as the provisions in the statute. Right to Information is very important for transparency in public administration.

Therefore, the success of this Bill mainly depends upon the success of the Right to Information Act. If it is not properly implemented, this Bill also will fail. At the same time, we have to form a Central Fund as well as a State Fund. Much depends upon the cooperation of the States concerned. There also, the same scheme will have to be implemented. There must be Committees in the States just as in the Centre. We have different political arrangements in different States. How far the States will cooperate is a matter to be decided in future. Without the States’ cooperation, this Bill cannot be implemented. These are the bottlenecks, these are the hardships which come to my mind when I think about the implementation of the National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill.

I wish the Government all success. I also give them my wholehearted support, but they would not get support as is expected in the Bill from all the States. So, they have to create a situation through which this Bill can be implemented. For that purpose, we must deal with this implementation, irrespective of political affiliations and irrespective of colour. We should have an independent approach, so far as implementation of this Bill is concerned.

I hope that the UPA Government will take the lead in getting cooperation or eliciting the cooperation of all the States in India. I hope, my learned friend, the Minister, will give emphasis and also will take sufficient precaution in getting or eliciting the support of all the States concerned without which we cannot implement this Bill.

With these words, I support the Bill.

DR. THOKCHOM MEINYA Mr. Deputy Speaker Sir, I do rise to support this historical bill The National Rural Employment Guarantee Bill, 2004 as moved by Hon’ble Minister Shri Raghuvansh Prasad Singh ji.

Sir, It is indeed heartening to see such a milestone piece of work in the history of Independent India. This is exactly the direct outcome of the National Common Minimum Programme of the United Progressive Alliance Government. Kudos! To the Hon’ble Chairperson of UPA the Hon’ble Prime Minister and the Hon’ble Rural Development Minister for this momentous piece of legislation.

Sir, I shall confine myself tot he execution part of the Act. The beginning shows the light. In the first place, two hundred districts will be covered and the remaining districts of the country in the coming five years. Sir, I would like to request the Union Government and the Rural Development Ministry in particular is include at least four districts from the State of Manipur – two each from the valley and the hills in the first instant.

Sir, the implementation of the provisions of the Act may be judiciously monitored. The country is marching ahead towards eradication of poverty-Garibi Hatao through Bharat Nirman Jai Hind.
